title: Help Me Do It on My Own: Sensory Data Analysis with jamovi and the SEDA Module
text:
Preface
This booklet was born from a simple conviction: we learn better to do things on our own when someone has taken the time to explain not only how, but also why.
The statistical analysis of sensory data has long been learned in R, through books, scripts, and tutorials that assumed a certain familiarity with programming, packages, and sometimes even a degree of resilience in the face of error messages. These tools have their strengths, their elegance, and remain indispensable. But they can also be a barrier for many practitioners who nevertheless work regularly with sensory data, without coming from the world of statistics or coding.
jamovi has partly changed the situation. By making methods accessible through its interface that were once reserved for more technical users, it has widened access to the statistical analysis of sensory data. But making a method clickable is not enough to make it understandable. A button without explanation remains a black box; a result without a reading framework remains fragile; a map without interpretation remains mute.
This is precisely the space this booklet seeks to occupy.
It replaces neither a full statistics course nor in-depth training in R. Its ambition is more focused: to give you, for each analysis, enough understanding to work with discernment. Enough to know what a confidence ellipse really represents. Enough to understand why a product may be absent from a descriptive table without thereby being “without a profile”. Enough not to read a preference map as an absolute truth far from the products actually tested. Enough, above all, no longer to be entirely dependent on an interface that one uses without understanding.
The guiding thread of this book is therefore autonomy. Not the immediate autonomy of someone who already knows everything, but the gradual autonomy of someone who can move forward with reliable points of reference, connect the visible options in jamovi to their statistical logic, and interpret the outputs more accurately. In that sense, this booklet deliberately sits between two worlds: that of concrete practice in jamovi, and that of methodological understanding, which gives meaning to the results.
This booklet covers the seven analyses of the SEDA module, in the following order: univariate characterisation of the product space, multivariate representation with confidence ellipses, CATA data analysis, JAR data analysis, Napping, free sorting, and finally preference mapping. Together, they form a coherent progression: from fixed-list attribute methods to more holistic approaches, and then to hedonic analyses. Each method corresponds to a particular way of producing data, asking a question, and interpreting a result. You can easily try these methods using the datasets distributed with the SEDA module, making it easier to become familiar with the graphs and outputs generated by each analysis.
To maintain overall coherence, each chapter follows the same structure: an introduction that sets out the statistical problem, a section explaining what is really happening behind the interface, a detailed presentation of the options, a step-by-step procedure, and then keys for interpreting the tables and graphs. This choice is not merely editorial; it is pedagogical. It is intended to ensure that, from one chapter to the next, the reader finds stable reference points and can more easily transfer what has been learned.
This booklet is intended for sensory evaluation practitioners, engineers, students, teachers, researchers discovering jamovi, and more broadly for anyone who needs support between a course and a real field analysis.
Each chapter can be read independently. You can enter this booklet through the method that corresponds to the data you currently have. But the whole has also been conceived as a journey: the further one goes, the more one understands that sensory analysis is not a stack of separate techniques, but a family of complementary approaches, articulated through common logics of representation, description, and interpretation.
At heart, this book pursues a very simple idea: a good tool should not merely make it possible to obtain a result, but should help one understand what that result means. If these pages allow you to move from “show me how to do it” to “now I can do it on my own”, then they will have fully achieved their purpose.

1.1.1 What is jamovi?
In one sentence: jamovi is a free, modern, and accessible statistics package, designed for both teaching and research.
Developed by contributors from the JASP project, jamovi relies on R for its statistical calculations while providing a graphical interface that requires no code at all. In practical terms, its interface works like a dynamic spreadsheet1: the data are visible and editable in a sheet on the left, and the results update in real time on the right. This organisation makes the tool accessible to both beginners and experienced users.
One often underestimated advantage of jamovi is its ability to save everything in a single .omv file: the data, the analysis options selected, and the results. This greatly facilitates reproducibility and the sharing of work, two areas in which traditional spreadsheets show their limits.

What about XLSTAT? XLSTAT is a paid-for Excel plug-in that adds advanced statistical functions. Although it is powerful, it remains proprietary, dependent on Microsoft Excel, and its cost may be a barrier for students or organisations with limited budgets. jamovi offers comparable features, and in some areas superior ones, while being entirely free and independent.


1.1.2 How do you install jamovi?
Installation is straightforward and requires no technical skills. jamovi is cross-platform: it works in the same way on Windows, macOS, and Linux. To install it, go to jamovi.org/download, choose your operating system, then run the downloaded file.
On the download page, two versions are offered. The Solid version is the most stable and thoroughly tested: it is the one to favour for teaching, practical classes, and research. The Current version includes the very latest features but may contain a few minor instabilities.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 The SEDA module
SEDA (Sensory Evaluation Data Analysis) is the jamovi module dedicated to the statistical analysis of sensory data. It is based on the R package SensoMineR and makes the main statistical methods used in sensory analysis available through a graphical interface — without requiring a single line of code.
Its menu is organised into three sections corresponding to three broad ways of producing sensory data.
The first section, Fixed List of Attributes, brings together methods in which subjects evaluate stimuli using a list of attributes defined in advance. This is the classic case of QDA (Quantitative Descriptive Analysis) data, where a trained panel scores the intensity of each attribute for each product. Here, SEDA offers two complementary analyses: one to characterise the stimuli attribute by attribute (by identifying which attributes differentiate them and which characterise each stimulus in particular), and another to represent the sensory space in a multivariate way (by producing a map of the stimuli enriched with confidence ellipses reflecting the stability of the positions according to panel composition). This section also includes the analysis of CATA (Check-All-That-Apply) data, in which respondents tick from a list the terms they feel are present in a stimulus, and the analysis of JAR (Just About Right) data, in which respondents indicate whether each attribute is too strong, too weak, or just about right — making it possible to estimate the penalties these deviations impose on liking.
The second section brings together holistic approaches, in which subjects evaluate the stimuli globally, without any predefined list of attributes. Two methods are covered: Napping (projective mapping), in which each subject positions the stimuli on a rectangle according to their perceived similarities, and free sorting (sorting task), in which each subject freely groups the stimuli into categories. In both cases, SEDA produces a consensual representation of the stimuli by combining the individual maps — by Multiple Factor Analysis for Napping, and by Multiple Correspondence Analysis for free sorting — and may complement this representation with an automatic classification of the stimuli.
The third section, Hedonic Data, is dedicated to liking data. It contains preference mapping, which combines an already constructed representation space (for example, from a PCA) with individual liking scores in order to identify favourable regions of that space. SEDA can also classify consumers from their centred liking profiles and produce preference maps for the resulting segments. This analysis is the natural extension of the previous analyses: once the sensory space has been constructed and interpreted, preference mapping helps identify which regions are favourable and whether the same preference structure is shared across consumer segments.
This booklet covers all seven of these analyses, in the order of the SEDA menu. Throughout the rest of this booklet, the terms product and stimulus mean the same thing and are used interchangeably.

1.4 From jamovi to R: the Rj Editor
SEDA can display the R script corresponding to the options selected in the interface. Throughout this booklet, these scripts provide a bridge from a point-and-click analysis to a reproducible R workflow.
Before using the Rj Editor for the first time, open its settings with the gear icon and select System R rather than jamovi R. Your system R installation must contain the packages required by the analysis — mainly SensoMineR and FactoMineR in this booklet — as well as jmvconnect, which gives the Rj Editor access to the dataset currently open in jamovi under the name data.
When an analysis offers the R code option, check it to display a script that can be copied into the Rj Editor. The chapters below explain the main functions and arguments used by each generated script.

title: 2  QDA Data — Characterisation of the Sensory Space
text:
2.1 Introduction
This analysis is designed for QDA (Quantitative Descriptive Analysis) data, when several subjects evaluate several stimuli using a fixed list of sensory attributes. It answers two complementary questions: which attributes structure the sensory space as a whole and which attributes characterise each stimulus in particular. More specifically, the function returns two families of results: a ranked list of the attributes that differentiate the set of stimuli, then, for each stimulus, a list of the attributes that characterise it.
Why not use a standard alternative?
A simple comparison of means by stimulus can be misleading if subjects do not all use the rating scale in the same way. Here, the analysis takes into account both the product effect (Stimulus Effect) and the subject effect (Subject Effect), which makes it possible to identify discriminating attributes and profiles more robustly than with a purely descriptive reading.
To test this function, simply load the sensochoc data available with the SEDA module — they appear in the list of example datasets when opening a new file in jamovi.

section: 2.2 Understanding what happens under the hood
text:
2.2 Understanding what happens under the hood

2.2.1 Data checking and preparation
The analysis first checks that the variable placed in the Stimulus Effect field and the variable placed in the Subject Effect field can be treated as factors, and that all variables placed in Sensory Attributes are numeric. If a sensory attribute is not numeric, the analysis stops with an error message.


2.2.2 An attribute-by-attribute analysis
A simple way to understand the computation is to say that the function proceeds attribute by attribute using an analysis of variance (ANOVA). For each variable in Sensory Attributes, it first evaluates whether the product effect is significant, while taking the subject effect into account. This first step acts as a global filter: it determines which attributes truly structure the sensory space.


2.2.3 Selection of discriminating attributes
Attributes whose significance is below the threshold defined by Significance threshold (%) are retained in the first results table. The default threshold is 5%, which makes it a good starting point for a cautious reading. If no attribute passes this threshold, the function stops and indicates that no sensory attribute is discriminating at the selected threshold.


2.2.4 Stimulus-by-stimulus description
Once the globally discriminating attributes have been identified, the function examines, for each stimulus, which attributes significantly characterise it. Each stimulus is compared with a global reference, which makes it possible to identify attributes positively or negatively associated with that stimulus. The global reference corresponds to the mean of the stimuli on each attribute, that is, the average stimulus. The result takes the form of a second table grouped by stimulus.


2.2.5 The role of adjusted means
The Adjusted mean column can be understood as an estimate of the stimulus mean on an attribute, corrected for the subject effect. This column makes it possible to read the perceived level of a stimulus without being limited to a raw mean that may be influenced by subjects who are more “generous” or more “severe” in their ratings.

When the tasting design is complete, that is, when each subject evaluates all stimuli, the adjusted mean is equal to the arithmetic mean. It differs from it when data are missing; in that case, the adjusted mean is more reliable.



2.2.6 What it means when a stimulus is absent from the second table, Sensory Description of the Stimuli
A stimulus may not appear in the second table if no attribute significantly characterises it at the chosen threshold. This does not mean that it has “no profile”, but rather that it does not differ clearly enough from the mean of the full set of stimuli on the tested attributes.

text:
2.4 Interface guide
The analysis appears in the menu SEDA > Fixed List of Attributes > Characterization of the Stimulus Space. The interface includes three variable drop zones, an Instructions and R Code section containing the Read me before running and R code checkboxes, and a numeric field, Significance threshold (%).

2.4.1 Variables to complete

2.4.1.1 Stimulus Effect
Role: identifies the stimuli/products to compare. Impact on the computation: this variable defines the groups studied in the global analysis and in the stimulus-by-stimulus description. Practical tip: use explicit labels, because they directly structure the reading of the second table.


2.4.1.2 Subject Effect
Role: identifies the subjects. Impact on the computation: this variable is used to take systematic differences between subjects into account when estimating stimulus effects. Practical tip: check that the same subject keeps exactly the same identifier throughout the file.


2.4.1.3 Sensory Attributes
Role: groups together the sensory attributes to be analysed. Impact on the computation: the function applies the same analysis logic to each of these attributes; only numeric attributes are accepted. Practical tip: include all relevant attributes from your QDA; the statistical selection will then be performed through Significance threshold (%).



2.4.2 Instructions and R Code

2.4.2.1 Read me before running
Role: displays integrated help in the results. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: leave it checked during the first uses. It is enabled by default.


2.4.2.2 R code
Role: displays the R script corresponding to the analysis in an R Code output. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: enable this option if you want to reproduce the analysis in the jamovi Rj Editor or continue working in R. It is disabled by default.



2.4.3 Significance threshold: Significance threshold (%)
Role: sets the p-value threshold used to select discriminating attributes and the attributes characteristic of each stimulus. Impact on the computation: this threshold controls both which attributes appear in Identification of the Sensory Dimensions (global test) and which attributes appear in Sensory Description of the Stimuli (stimulus-level tests). A low threshold produces more conservative results; a higher threshold retains more attributes in both tables. Practical tip: the default value is 5%, a good starting point for a first trial. If the results are too sparse, try 10%, then possibly 20% for exploratory work.

title: 2  QDA Data — Characterisation of the Sensory Space
text:
2.5 Step-by-step procedure

Open your dataset in jamovi.
In the Data tab, check that the stimulus variable is categorical, that the subject variable is categorical, and that the sensory attributes are numeric.
Open SEDA > Fixed List of Attributes > Characterization of the Stimulus Space.
Place the stimulus variable in Stimulus Effect.
Place the subject variable in Subject Effect.
Place all sensory attributes in Sensory Attributes.
Leave Significance threshold (%) at 5% for a first trial.
First read Identification of the Sensory Dimensions to identify the attributes that structure the sensory space.
Then read Sensory Description of the Stimuli to understand the characteristics specific to each stimulus.
If no results appear, or if the second table is very sparse, test a slightly broader threshold.

title: 2  QDA Data — Characterisation of the Sensory Space
text:
2.6 Interpretation of results

2.6.1 Identification of the Sensory Dimensions
This first table lists the sensory attributes that significantly discriminate the stimuli, sorted from the most discriminating to the least discriminating. It is the entry point for interpretation: it indicates which attributes structure the sensory space as a whole.







Element
Meaning




(first column)
Discriminating sensory attribute


Vtest
Standardised measure of the discriminating effect — the higher the value, the stronger the signal


p
P-value of the global test — the lower it is, the more clearly the attribute differentiates the stimuli



The first rows of the table correspond to the most structuring attributes.

Point of vigilance: an attribute absent from this table is not sufficiently discriminating at the chosen threshold. If no attribute is retained, the function displays an error message and does not produce interpretable results.



2.6.2 Sensory Description of the Stimuli
This second table describes each stimulus through the attributes that significantly characterise it. Rows are grouped by stimulus, and the most salient attributes appear first within each group.







Element
Meaning




(first column)
Name of the stimulus


Descriptor
Characteristic sensory attribute


Coefficient
Estimated deviation from the global reference — positive if the stimulus is perceived more intensely, negative otherwise


Adjusted mean
Adjusted mean of the stimulus on this attribute, corrected for the subject effect


p
P-value of the characterisation test


Vtest
Standardised intensity of the association — positive = over-represented, negative = under-represented




A positive V-test suggests that the stimulus is perceived as more intense than the reference, that is, the mean, on this attribute.
A negative V-test suggests the opposite — and is just as informative.
Use Adjusted mean to read the sensory level, but never interpret it without p and Vtest.


Point of vigilance: a stimulus absent from the table does not have “no profile”; it is simply not significantly different from the mean of the full set of stimuli at the chosen threshold.

In the current configuration of the function, no graphical output is produced. Interpretation is based entirely on the two result tables.

title: 2  QDA Data — Characterisation of the Sensory Space
text:
2.7 Example: the sensochoc dataset
The sensochoc dataset describes 6 chocolates evaluated by 29 subjects on 14 sensory attributes. It is used to illustrate the function outputs. The numerical values discussed below come directly from the analysis results. To load this dataset, open jamovi, click the icon in the top left corner, the three stacked lines, then Open → Data Library → SEDA.

2.7.1 Example settings
To reproduce this example, use the following values.



Option
Value




Stimulus Effect
Product


Subject Effect
Panelist


Sensory Attributes
all numeric sensory attributes


Significance threshold (%)
5





2.7.2 Analysis of the Identification of the Sensory Dimensions table
With these settings, all 14 attributes emerge as discriminating at the 5% threshold. The table is sorted by decreasing V-test: the attributes at the top are those that most clearly differentiate the chocolates from one another. MilkF comes first (V-test = 16.40), followed by CocoaF (13.48) and Bitterness (13.34). At the bottom of the table, Sticky (V-test = 3.56) and Granular (4.37) are significant but less structuring. This ranking provides a first reading of the sensory space: the contrasts between chocolates are based above all on milky, cocoa, and bitter dimensions.


2.7.3 Analysis of the Sensory Description of the Stimuli table
The second table makes it possible to read the profile of each chocolate relative to the overall mean of all six chocolates.
choc1 is characterised by a highly contrasted profile. For this chocolate, on the positive side, Bitterness has the highest V-test (9.95, coefficient +2.46) and an adjusted mean of 7.07, clearly above the overall mean. CocoaF (V-test = 8.48), Astringency (7.08), and Acidity (6.14) complete this profile. On the negative side, Sweetness (V-test = -8.29, coefficient -1.95, adjusted mean 3.14) and MilkF (V-test = -8.70) indicate a chocolate that is very low in sweetness and very low in milky notes.
choc3 presents the opposite profile. It is strongly characterised by MilkF (V-test = 16.52, the highest in the table), Caramel (11.52), Sweetness (10.39), and Melting (9.19). Conversely, it is negatively characterised by Bitterness (-12.42), Crunchy (-12.49), and CocoaF (-13.33). It is the milkiest, sweetest, and most melting chocolate, and the least bitter and cocoa-like. Given the number of significant sensory attributes, choc3 appears to be the chocolate whose profile differs most clearly from the mean.
choc2 stands out mainly through Crunchy (V-test = 6.92) and a lower perception of MilkF (-5.16). choc6 is also Crunchy (5.35) and slightly more Sweetness (2.41), but less Melting (-3.08).
choc4 shows a moderate and weakly contrasted profile — except for MilkF, no V-test exceeds 4 in absolute value — which suggests a chocolate close to the general sensory mean on most attributes.
choc5 has very few salient characteristics: only CocoaA, Crunchy, and CocoaF appear slightly on the positive side, and Sticky on the negative side. Its profile is the least distinctive of the six chocolates at the 5% threshold.


2.7.4 Synthetic interpretation
This example shows that the six chocolates cover a broad sensory space, with a very bitter and intense chocolate at one extreme (choc1) and a milky, sweet, and melting chocolate at the other (choc3). Between these two poles, the other chocolates occupy more intermediate positions. The first table identifies the attributes that globally structure the sensory space, while the second specifies the profile specific to each stimulus. The joint reading of these two outputs is the main contribution of the function.

What we take away from this example: the analysis combines a global reading of discriminating attributes and a local reading of stimulus profiles, making it possible to characterise the sensory space in detail.

2.8 From jamovi to the Rj Editor
Once the Rj Editor has been configured with System R as described in Chapter 1, check R code to display the script corresponding to the analysis. The dataset currently open in jamovi is available as data.
For this analysis, the script loads SensoMineR, prepares the selected variables, and then calls decat() with a model including the stimulus and subject effects. The value of Significance threshold (%) is passed to the proba argument: 5% in the interface becomes 0.05 in R. The objects res_QDA$resF and res_QDA$resT correspond respectively to the two tables discussed in this chapter.
This output provides a way to inspect and reproduce the computation and, when useful, continue the analysis in R. It is not required to use SEDA.

title: 2  QDA Data — Characterisation of the Sensory Space
text:
2.9 Practical tips

Start with Significance threshold (%) = 5%.
If no attribute is retained, test 10%, then 20% for exploratory work.
Always read the global table before the stimulus-by-stimulus table.
Do not confuse a globally discriminating attribute with an attribute that strongly characterises all stimuli: an attribute can differentiate stimuli from one another without all of them being strongly associated with it.
A negative V-test is informative: it indicates that a stimulus is perceived as less intense than the mean on an attribute, which can be a sensory characteristic in its own right.
Use clear and consistent stimulus names to make the results easier to read.
If your panel includes repetitions, keep all rows in the file.
Do not overinterpret the absence of a stimulus from the second table: it may simply be located close to the general sensory mean.

2.10 In summary
This analysis first identifies the sensory attributes that globally discriminate the stimuli, then describes each stimulus through the attributes that distinguish it from the global reference, that is, the mean. It takes into account both the stimulus effect and the subject effect, which makes it more informative than a simple comparison of raw means. Its main value is that it combines a global reading of the sensory space and a local stimulus-by-stimulus reading, in two directly interpretable tables.

title: 3  QDA Data — Multivariate Representation with Ellipses
text:
3.1 Introduction
This analysis is designed for Quantitative Descriptive Analysis (QDA) data, that is, when several subjects evaluate several stimuli using a fixed list of sensory attributes. It extends the univariate characterisation of the sensory space by providing a multivariate representation of the stimuli and their variability. It answers two complementary questions: which stimuli are sensorially similar and is this proximity stable despite variability between subjects? Its central output is a map of the stimuli enriched with ellipses, which visualise not only the position of the stimuli, but also the robustness of this position under panel resampling.
Why not use a standard alternative?
A PCA applied directly to the raw data may mix two sources of variation: the stimulus effect and the subject effect. In sensory analysis, some subjects systematically rate higher or lower than others, or use the scale more or less broadly. This analysis takes this subject/stimulus structure into account to produce a representation better suited to QDA data.

title: 3  QDA Data — Multivariate Representation with Ellipses
section: 3.2 Understanding what happens under the hood
text:
3.2 Understanding what happens under the hood

3.2.1 Selection of sensory attributes
Before constructing the map, the function identifies the attributes that discriminate the stimuli sufficiently. This selection depends on the value of Descriptor selection threshold (%). The stricter the threshold, the more streamlined the map will be; the broader it is, the more exhaustive the representation will be, although sometimes more crowded. The default value is 20%, which makes it a good starting point for exploration.


3.2.2 Correction of the subject effect
A simple way to understand the next step is to say that the analysis reconstructs mean sensory profiles by stimulus, while taking differences between subjects into account. Two options are involved here:

Center by subject corrects differences in average level between subjects;
Scale by subject corrects differences in the amplitude with which subjects use the scale.

The objective is to prevent a very generous, very severe, or very “spread-out” subject from artificially distorting the map of the stimuli.


3.2.3 Principal component analysis
A PCA is then performed on the resulting table of sensory profiles. It produces the stimulus map, the sensory attribute map, the eigenvalue table, and the automatic description of the dimensions. This factor space is then used as the reference space for projecting the virtual panels.


3.2.4 Virtual panels and supplementary individuals
The key point of the function is the use of resampling. In PCA, it is possible to distinguish between active individuals — those used to construct the axes — and supplementary individuals — those projected afterwards, without modifying the axes. This is precisely the mechanism that makes it possible to construct the ellipses.
At each simulation, a subset of subjects is drawn with replacement from the original panel, new mean stimulus profiles are recalculated, and then projected into the factor space as supplementary individuals. The dispersion of these projections around each stimulus is then summarised by an ellipse.
These ellipses therefore describe the variability of the mean position of the stimuli when the composition of the panel changes, not the simple raw dispersion of individual ratings.

Note: the computation may take a few seconds, because it relies on a large number of virtual panels. During this computation, it is better to avoid changing other options so as not to restart the procedure unnecessarily.



3.2.5 Comparison between stimuli
The function also computes a comparison between pairs of stimuli, presented as a matrix of p-values. The Hotelling test is performed on the selected factor plane defined by X-axis and Y-axis. This output complements the visual reading of the ellipses; the pairwise comparisons are exploratory and are reported without multiplicity adjustment.


3.2.6 Automatic description of the dimensions
Finally, the function provides an automatic description of the axes, filtered according to the value of Significance threshold (%). It helps identify which attributes are most strongly associated with each dimension and gives a sensory meaning to the axes.

3.4 Interface guide
The analysis appears in the menu SEDA > Fixed List of Attributes > Representation of the Stimulus Space. The interface includes three variable drop zones, an Instructions and R Code section containing the Read me before running and R code checkboxes, and then three collapsible menus: Graphic Options, Resampling Options, and Numerical Indicators.

3.4.1 Variables to complete

3.4.1.1 Stimulus Effect
Role: identifies the stimuli to be represented on the map. Impact on the computation: each level of this variable becomes a mean point and, where applicable, an ellipse on the map. Practical tip: use clear labels, because they will appear directly in the graphics.


3.4.1.2 Subject Effect
Role: identifies the subjects. Impact on the computation: this variable is essential for correcting the subject effect and for generating the virtual panels used in the bootstrap. Practical tip: check that the same subject keeps exactly the same identifier throughout the file.


3.4.1.3 Sensory Attributes
Role: groups together the sensory attributes used to construct the factor space. Impact on the computation: only numeric attributes are accepted; the number of calculable dimensions depends on the number of retained attributes. Practical tip: start by including all relevant sensory attributes, then refine the selection with Descriptor selection threshold (%).



3.4.2 Instructions and R Code

3.4.2.1 Read me before running
Role: displays integrated help in the results. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: leave it checked during the first uses. It is enabled by default.


3.4.2.2 R code
Role: displays the R script corresponding to the analysis in an R Code output. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: enable this option to reproduce the analysis in the Rj Editor or continue working in R. It is disabled by default.



3.4.3 Standardization of the Sensory Attributes: Scale to unit variance
Role: standardises the sensory attributes when performing the PCA. Impact on the computation: when checked, each attribute contributes equally to the construction of the axes; when unchecked, the most dispersed attributes have a greater influence on the construction of the axes. Practical tip: leave this option checked in most analyses. It is enabled by default.


3.4.4 Selection of the Sensory Attributes: Descriptor selection threshold (%)
Role: sets the threshold for selecting attributes according to their relationship with the stimulus effect. Impact on the computation: a low threshold retains few attributes and produces a more readable map; a higher threshold retains more attributes and gives a broader view. Practical tip: the default value is 20%, a good starting point for exploration. For a stricter version, start at 5%.


3.4.5 Graphic Options

3.4.5.1 Components to Plot — X-axis and Y-axis
Role: choose the dimensions displayed on the horizontal and vertical axes. Impact on the computation: they do not change the PCA itself, but they modify the displayed factor plane. The selected dimensions must exist in the analysis, otherwise the function generates an error. Practical tip: start with X-axis = 1 and Y-axis = 2, the default values.


3.4.5.2 Individual variability around stimuli
Role: adds a graph showing the dispersion of individual evaluations around each stimulus. Impact on the computation: it does not add a new analysis, but provides an additional graphical output useful for assessing consensus between subjects. Practical tip: activate this option if you want to distinguish a consensual stimulus from a stimulus perceived more variably. The default value is disabled.


3.4.5.3 Variability around sensory attributes
Role: adds a graph showing the variability of sensory attributes under resampling. Impact on the computation: it provides a graphical output useful for assessing the stability of attribute interpretation. Practical tip: activate this option when you want to comment on the robustness of the axes. The default value is disabled.



3.4.6 Resampling Options

3.4.6.1 Subjects per virtual panel
Role: defines the number of subjects drawn in each virtual panel. Impact on the computation: the closer this value is to the actual panel size, the more similar the simulated panels will be to it. Practical tip: use the actual panel size as a starting point. The default value is 20.


3.4.6.2 Number of virtual panels
Role: sets the total number of simulated virtual panels. Impact on the computation: the larger this number, the more stable the ellipses will be from one run to another, but computation time increases. Practical tip: 300 is a good compromise to start with; for a final rendering, it may be useful to increase this number to 500. The default value is 300.


3.4.6.3 Ellipse alpha (%)
Role: defines the alpha level used to draw the confidence ellipses. Impact on the computation: a lower alpha produces wider ellipses; with the default value of 5%, the ellipse corresponds to a 95% level in the covariance-based construction of the simulated positions. Practical tip: leave 5% for a first trial.


3.4.6.4 Center by subject
Role: centres responses subject by subject. Impact on the computation: corrects differences in average level between subjects and often improves the comparison between profiles. Practical tip: leave this option checked in almost all analyses. It is enabled by default.


3.4.6.5 Scale by subject
Role: standardises responses subject by subject. Impact on the computation: corrects differences in amplitude between subjects, but modifies the initial structure more strongly than centring alone. Practical tip: leave this option unchecked at first. It is disabled by default.



3.4.7 Numerical Indicators

3.4.7.1 Significance threshold (%)
Role: defines the significance threshold for the automatic description of the dimensions. Impact on the computation: the stricter the threshold, the more selective the automatic description will be. Practical tip: the default value, 5%, is well suited to a first reading.


3.4.7.2 Number of dimensions
Role: defines the number of dimensions included in the automatic description. Impact on the computation: SEDA computes enough components to describe these dimensions; the displayed plane is selected separately with X-axis and Y-axis. Practical tip: the default value, 2, is appropriate for an initial reading.

3.5 Step-by-step procedure

Open your dataset in jamovi.
In the Data tab, check that the stimulus variable is categorical, the subject variable is categorical, and the sensory attributes are numeric.
Open SEDA > Fixed List of Attributes > Representation of the Stimulus Space.
Place the stimulus variable in Stimulus Effect.
Place the subject variable in Subject Effect.
Place all sensory attributes in Sensory Attributes.
Leave Scale to unit variance checked.
Set Descriptor selection threshold (%) to 20% for an initial exploration, or to 5% for a stricter selection.
Keep X-axis = 1 and Y-axis = 2.
Leave Center by subject checked and Scale by subject unchecked at first.
Set Subjects per virtual panel to the panel size or a close value, leave Number of virtual panels at 300 and Ellipse alpha (%) at 5.
Activate Individual variability around stimuli and/or Variability around sensory attributes according to your needs.
In Numerical Indicators, keep the default values for a first trial.
First read Representation of the Stimuli and Representation of the Sensory Attributes, then Eigenvalue Decomposition and Automatic Description of the Dimensions. Next assess stability with Representation of the Stimuli with Confidence Ellipses and Hotelling Test.
Then return to the settings to test the stability of your conclusions.

title: 3  QDA Data — Multivariate Representation with Ellipses
text:
3.6 Interpretation of results

3.6.1 Representation of the Stimuli with Confidence Ellipses
This is the central graph of the function. Each stimulus is represented by a mean point in the factor space, surrounded by an ellipse. The axes come from the PCA, and the percentage displayed on each axis indicates the share of variance explained.







Element
Meaning




Two close stimuli
Similar sensory profiles


Strongly overlapping ellipses
Less clear visual separation under resampling


Small ellipse
Position stable across simulated panels


Large ellipse
More uncertain position


Clearly separated ellipses
Clearer visual separation under resampling




Point of vigilance: the ellipses describe the variability of the mean position of the stimuli under panel resampling. They do not directly represent the raw dispersion of individual ratings. Ellipse overlap is a visual guide, not a significance test; use the Hotelling Test for the pairwise statistical comparison.



3.6.2 Representation of the Stimuli
This map shows the relative positions of the stimuli without emphasizing the ellipses. It is useful for quickly identifying the main groupings and oppositions between stimuli.


3.6.3 Representation of the Sensory Attributes
This map shows the sensory attributes in the factor space. It is read using three simple cues:

direction: toward which stimuli the attribute “pulls” the structure;
length: the longer an attribute is, the better it is represented on the plane;
the angle between two attributes: small angle = positive correlation; angle close to 180° = opposition; angle close to 90° = near-independence.

This is the map that gives sensory meaning to the axes.


3.6.4 Individual variability around stimuli (available only if the option is activated)
This output shows the dispersion of individual evaluations around the mean point of each stimulus. A compact cloud indicates strong consensus; a dispersed cloud indicates a more heterogeneous perception between subjects.


3.6.5 Variability of the Sensory Attributes (available only if the option is activated)
This output shows the dispersion of the position of sensory attributes in the virtual panels. A compact cloud means that the attribute is stable; a dispersed cloud indicates that its interpretation is more fragile and depends more strongly on the composition of the panel.


3.6.6 Eigenvalue Decomposition
This table gives, for each dimension, the eigenvalue, the percentage of variance explained, and the cumulative percentage. If the first two dimensions explain a large share of the variance, the 2D map summarises the data well. Otherwise, it is prudent to explore other planes, for example Dim 1 / Dim 3.


3.6.7 Automatic Description of the Dimensions
This table identifies the attributes most strongly linked to each dimension, filtered by Significance threshold (%). It reports, in particular, their correlation with the dimension and the associated p-value. A dimension requested in Number of dimensions may not appear if no attribute reaches the selected significance threshold. The table helps give the axes a sensory interpretation and complements the attribute map.


3.6.8 Hotelling Test
This p-value matrix compares each pair of stimuli on the selected factor plane defined by X-axis and Y-axis. A low p-value provides evidence of separation between two stimuli on that plane; a high p-value does not establish such separation. These pairwise comparisons are exploratory and are reported without multiplicity adjustment. The table therefore complements the visual reading of the ellipses rather than replacing it.

Reproducibility note: the numerical results and resampling-based plots discussed below were generated with the default value Subjects per virtual panel = 20. Use 20 to reproduce this chapter exactly. Because the actual panel contains 29 subjects, 29 is a natural choice for a new final analysis; changing this value changes the resampling-based outputs.



3.7.2 Analysis of the Representation of the Stimuli with Confidence Ellipses graph
The map shows the 6 chocolates in the Dim. 1 / Dim. 2 plane. The first dimension alone accounts for 88.79% of the total variance — this 2D plane is therefore a very faithful representation of the data. The second dimension explains an additional 7.58%.
On the horizontal axis (Dim. 1), choc1 and choc3 occupy the two opposite extremes: choc1 on the left (bitter, cocoa side), choc3 on the right (milky, sweet side). These are the two chocolates whose profiles are most clearly opposed, which is consistent with the results of the previous chapter. choc2, choc5, and choc6 are grouped in the centre, close to the origin. choc4 is located slightly above the horizontal axis, between choc1 and the central group.
The ellipses provide information about the robustness of these positions. The ellipses of choc2, choc5, and choc6 overlap widely: their visual separation is therefore less clear when panel composition changes. Conversely, choc1 and choc3 have ellipses clearly separated from all the others: their visual separation appears robust across the simulated panels. The Hotelling Test then provides the statistical assessment of these differences on the displayed plane.


3.7.3 Analysis of the Hotelling Test table
The p-value table quantitatively complements the ellipse reading on the Dim. 1 / Dim. 2 plane. The pairs choc2 / choc5 (p = 0.76) and choc5 / choc6 (p = 0.16) have high p-values: no separation is established between these chocolates on this plane. The pair choc2 / choc6 is more borderline (p = 0.04). Conversely, all comparisons involving choc1 or choc3 give p-values of 0.00 in the results of this example. These pairwise comparisons are exploratory and are not adjusted for multiplicity.


3.7.4 Analysis of the Representation of the Sensory Attributes graph
The 14 attributes are distributed very clearly around the horizontal axis. On the right are grouped MilkF, Sweetness, Caramel, Vanilla, MilkA, and Melting — this is the profile of choc3. On the left are grouped CocoaF, CocoaA, Bitterness, Astringency, Acidity, Crunchy, and Granular — this is the profile of choc1. The horizontal axis therefore clearly corresponds to an opposition between sweet milk chocolate / bitter dark chocolate.
The length of the arrows also indicates the quality of representation of each attribute on this plane. Crunchy has a shorter arrow pointing downward, indicating that it is less well represented on this plane than CocoaF or MilkF, whose arrows almost reach the edge of the circle. Arrow length does not, by itself, measure stability across panels; that question is addressed by the Variability of the Sensory Attributes plot.


3.7.5 Analysis of the Automatic Description of the Dimensions table
The automatic description of the dimensions confirms the very strong opposition carried by Dim. 1. The most positively correlated attributes are MilkF (1.00), MilkA (0.99), Caramel (0.99), Vanilla (0.98), and Sweetness (0.95). At the opposite end, the strongest negative correlations are observed for CocoaF (-1.00), Bitterness (-0.97), CocoaA (-0.97), Granular (-0.96), and Astringency (-0.94). With Significance threshold (%) = 5, no attribute is retained for Dim. 2 in this table.


3.7.6 Synthetic interpretation
The sensory space of the chocolates is very largely structured by a single strong opposition, carried by the first dimension: on one side, a milky, sweet, and melting profile; on the other, a bitter, cocoa, and more textured profile. The stimulus map and the attribute map converge toward the same overall reading. The ellipses additionally show that not all stimuli are differentiated with the same robustness. Finally, the Hotelling test confirms that some proximities observed on the map do not correspond to clearly established differences.

What we take away from this example: the analysis does not only show where the stimuli are located in the sensory space, but also how robustly they can be distinguished.

Always start with X-axis = 1 and Y-axis = 2.
Leave Scale to unit variance checked in most cases.
Use Center by subject almost systematically.

This analysis produces a multivariate representation of stimuli suited to QDA data, while taking the subject effect into account in the construction of sensory profiles. It enriches the classical factor map with ellipses obtained by resampling, making it possible to assess the robustness of the observed positions. It therefore shows not only where the stimuli are located, but also how confidently they can be located there.

title: 4  CATA Data — Analysis of Checked Terms
text:
4.1 Introduction
This analysis is designed for CATA (Check-All-That-Apply) data, that is, when subjects check, from a predefined list, all the terms they consider appropriate to describe a stimulus. It answers two complementary questions: which terms characterise each stimulus and how the stimuli are globally organised according to their CATA profiles. The function produces a contingency table, a description of the stimuli according to the CATA terms, as well as a correspondence analysis followed by a classification of the stimuli, automatic by default.
Why not use a standard alternative?
CATA data are originally binary responses by subject and by term. A classical comparison of means is therefore not the most suitable tool for representing the global structure of these data. The function first aggregates the responses into a stimuli × terms contingency table, then applies methods suited to this structure: frequency description, correspondence analysis, and, when possible, classification.

title: 4  CATA Data — Analysis of Checked Terms
section: 4.2 Understanding what happens under the hood
text:
4.2 Understanding what happens under the hood

4.2.1 Construction of the contingency table
The first step consists of grouping the responses by stimulus. The function sums the columns placed in the CATA field for each level of Stimulus Effect. This produces a table where rows are stimuli, columns are CATA terms, and each cell indicates how many times a term was checked for a given stimulus. This table is the basis for all subsequent outputs.

Note: this table can be copied into a spreadsheet file.



4.2.2 Description of stimuli by terms
From this contingency table, the function applies a frequency description procedure based on the threshold value defined in Significance threshold (%). For each stimulus, it identifies the terms that are significantly more or less frequent than in the whole table. This logic is close to a statistical description of profiles, but adapted here to checking frequencies rather than to continuous ratings. The same threshold is then applied to the description of clusters.

A term absent from the description table is not significantly associated with a stimulus at the chosen threshold. This may mean that it is checked fairly evenly across stimuli.



4.2.3 Correspondence analysis
If at least three variables are placed in the CATA field, the function performs a correspondence analysis on the contingency table. This method simultaneously represents the stimuli and the terms in the same factor space. Two stimuli that are close on the map tend to share similar CATA profiles; two terms that are close tend to be checked for similar stimuli. The axes summarise the main profile oppositions between stimuli and terms.


4.2.4 Classification of stimuli
Once the correspondence analysis has been computed, the function runs a hierarchical clustering on principal components (HCPC). By default, Number of clusters = -1 lets FactoMineR determine the number of groups automatically, but the user can also impose a number of clusters. The clustering uses the first CA dimensions defined by Number of dimensions for clustering; this setting is distinct from the factor plane displayed with X-axis and Y-axis. The percentages displayed on the HCPC map are expressed relative to the inertia of this retained clustering space and may therefore differ from those on the full CA map.
The function then produces a map of the stimuli according to their clusters and a description of the clusters using the same significance threshold as for the description of stimuli.


4.2.5 Minimum conditions for running the analysis
SEDA requires at least three CATA variables. With fewer than three attributes, the analysis stops. To construct a two-dimensional correspondence-analysis map, the aggregated table must also contain at least three stimuli and three informative CATA attributes.
CATA variables must be complete 0/1 indicators: 0 means that the term was not checked and 1 that it was checked. Missing values are not interpreted as unchecked responses and must be resolved before the analysis.

4.4 Interface guide
The analysis appears in the menu SEDA > Fixed List of Attributes > Analysis of CATA Data. The interface includes two variable drop zones, an Instructions and R Code section, the Significance threshold (%) field, and two collapsible menus: Graphic Options and Clustering.

4.4.1 Variables to complete

4.4.1.1 Stimulus Effect
Role: identifies the stimuli to compare. Impact on the computation: this variable defines the rows of the contingency table and organises all descriptive and graphical outputs. Practical tip: use clear labels, because they will appear in the tables and graphs.


4.4.1.2 CATA
Role: groups together the terms from the CATA list. Impact on the computation: these variables define the columns of the contingency table; they are then used for stimulus description, correspondence analysis, and clustering. Practical tip: select at least three complete CATA variables coded as 0/1.



4.4.2 Instructions and R Code

4.4.2.1 Read me before running
Role: displays integrated help in the results. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: leave it checked during the first uses. It is enabled by default.


4.4.2.2 R code
Role: displays the R script corresponding to the analysis in an R Code output. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: enable this option to reproduce the analysis in the Rj Editor or continue working in R. It is disabled by default.



4.4.3 Significance threshold (%)
Role: defines the p-value threshold used to select terms characterising stimuli and clusters. Impact on the computation: this threshold affects the descfreq description tables but does not change the construction of the correspondence analysis or the clustering. Practical tip: the default value is 5%.


4.4.4 Graphic Options

4.4.4.1 X-axis and Y-axis
Role: choose the two correspondence-analysis dimensions displayed on the maps. Impact on the computation: they change the displayed plane, not the CA structure itself. Practical tip: start with X-axis = 1 and Y-axis = 2, the default values.



4.4.5 Clustering

4.4.5.1 Number of dimensions for clustering
Role: sets the number of first CA dimensions used by HCPC. Impact on the computation: clustering may therefore use more information than the displayed plane alone. The default value is 5; if fewer than five dimensions are available, SEDA uses all available dimensions. Practical tip: the axes chosen for the graph must be included among the dimensions used for clustering.


4.4.5.2 Number of clusters
Role: sets the number of stimulus groups. Impact on the computation: with the default value -1, FactoMineR determines the number of clusters automatically; an integer value of at least 2 imposes that number of groups. The requested number must remain lower than the number of stimuli. Practical tip: start with -1, and impose a number of groups only when there is an analytical reason to do so.

4.6 Interpretation of results

4.6.1 Contingency table
This first table crosses stimuli in rows and CATA terms in columns. Each cell indicates the number of times a term was checked for a given stimulus.







Element
Meaning




High value in a cell
The term was often checked for this stimulus


Row with several high values
The stimulus is associated with several frequent terms


Column high for almost all stimuli
Frequent term, but not necessarily discriminating




Point of vigilance: a very frequent term is not automatically a characteristic term. If it is checked for almost all stimuli, it will contribute little to distinguishing them.



4.6.2 Description of the Stimuli According to CATA
This table describes each stimulus through the terms that are significantly associated with it, grouped by stimulus. Terms are sorted by decreasing V-test within each group.







Element
Meaning




(first column)
Stimulus concerned


CATA
Characteristic term


Intern %
Percentage of use of the term for this stimulus

Overall percentage of use of the term


Intern frequency
Absolute frequency of the term for this stimulus


Global frequency
Total absolute frequency of the term


p

A positive V-test indicates that the term is checked more frequently for this stimulus than overall.
A negative V-test indicates that it is checked less frequently — and is just as informative.
A low p-value indicates a clearer characterisation.


A stimulus absent from this table does not have “no profile”; it is simply close to the mean profile of all stimuli at the chosen threshold.



4.6.3 Representation of the Stimuli and the CATA (available with at least 3 terms)
This graph is produced only if at least three terms are placed in CATA. It simultaneously represents the stimuli and the terms in the factor space derived from the correspondence analysis.

Two close stimuli have similar CATA profiles.
Stimuli and terms should be interpreted relative to the factor dimensions and the oppositions they structure; a direct distance between a stimulus and a term should not be read as an ordinary Euclidean distance.
The percentage displayed on each axis indicates the share of total information captured by that dimension.

This map gives an overview, but it does not replace the descriptive table. The two should be read together.


4.6.4 Representation of the Stimuli According to Clusters (available with at least 3 terms)
This graph represents the stimuli according to the HCPC partition. With Number of clusters = -1, the partition is selected automatically; if a number of clusters is imposed, the map reflects that partition. Clustering uses the first dimensions defined by Number of dimensions for clustering, while X-axis and Y-axis determine the displayed plane. The percentages on the HCPC map refer to the retained clustering space, not to the full CA inertia.

Stimuli in the same cluster have similar CATA profiles.
Distant clusters correspond to more contrasted families of stimuli.
This output helps summarise the global structure of the stimuli.



4.6.5 Description of the Clusters (available with at least 3 terms)
When the classification is available, the function also produces a table describing each cluster through the terms that are significantly associated with it, using the same logic as for the description of stimuli.

text:
4.7 Example: the Giacalone_et_al_cata dataset
The Giacalone_et_al_cata dataset describes 9 beers evaluated by 74 consumers on 15 CATA items: here, the aim is to associate beers with particular occasions. It is used to illustrate the function outputs. The numerical values and graphics discussed below come directly from the analysis results. To load this dataset, open jamovi, click the icon in the top left corner, the three stacked lines, then Open → Data Library → SEDA.

4.7.1 Example settings
To reproduce this example, use the following values.







Option
Value




Stimulus Effect
Product


CATA
all CATA items from ThirstQ to Concert


Significance threshold (%)
5


X-axis / Y-axis
1 / 2


Number of dimensions for clustering
5


Number of clusters
-1 (automatic)





4.7.2 Analysis of the Description of the Stimuli According to CATA table
The table allows a stimulus-by-stimulus reading with test values and actual frequencies.
GMA is significantly characterised by Rugby (V-test = 3.95, p < .001; 11.61% versus 7.08% overall) and CampingFishing (2.73, p = 0.006). Conversely, it is under-represented by Gift (V-test = -4.36), Treat (-3.84), and FineDinning (-3.51) — all highly significant.
LR has the profile most strongly marked by Rugby in the whole set (V-test = 5.74, p < .001; 15.24% versus 7.08% overall) and CampingFishing (2.83). It is under-represented by Guests (-4.77), FineDinning (-3.91), Treat (-3.74), and Gift (-3.50).
SSA stands out from all other stimuli by the intensity of its positive associations: Gift (V-test = 6.43, p < .001; 13.41% versus 4.21% overall), FineDinning (6.09), Treat (4.53), Achievement (3.71), and Guests (2.72). Conversely, it is strongly under-represented by Rugby (-4.29), ThirstQ (-3.63), Work (-3.01), CampingFishing (-2.88), and TV (-2.80). It is the stimulus whose profile differs most clearly from the mean.
SC is more strongly linked to Rugby (2.82) and ThirstQ (2.69), and is under-represented by PubHouse (-2.67), Treat (-2.58), and Gift (-2.55).
HPW is more strongly associated with Treat (V-test = 2.41) and Gift (2.21), and is under-represented by Rugby (-3.29). PKB is more strongly associated with Gift (2.60) and Treat (2.10); no negative term reaches the 5% threshold for this stimulus.
MBB mainly stands out through PubHouse (2.62) and is negatively distinguished by ThirstQ (-2.35) and Rugby (-2.19).
STG is characterised only by Rugby on the negative side (-2.75, p = 0.006).


4.7.3 Analysis of the Representation of the Stimuli and the CATA graph
The first dimension explains 85.59% of the inertia — a remarkably high value, meaning that the main opposition between stimuli is very strong and very readable on the horizontal axis. The second dimension explains only 7.43%, but refines secondary distinctions.
On the map, SSA is located very clearly on the right, isolated near Gift, FineDinning, and Achievement. On the left are grouped LR, GMA, and SC, close to Rugby and CampingFishing. MBB, HPW, PKB, MHR, and STG occupy a central or slightly right-hand position, between the two poles. On the second dimension, LR is located slightly higher than GMA and SC, which reflects its stronger association with Rugby.


4.7.4 Analysis of the Representation of the Stimuli According to Clusters and the Description of the Clusters graph and table
The automatic classification retains three clusters:

Cluster 1 (black): LR, GMA, and SC — positively characterised by Rugby (V-test = 9.12, p < .001), CampingFishing (4.86), ThirstQ (3.81), and TV (3.01), and under-represented notably by Gift (-6.97), Treat (-6.81), FineDinning (-6.21), and Guests (-4.67). This cluster corresponds to the pole most strongly associated with sports and outdoor contexts.
Cluster 2 (red): MBB, HPW, PKB, MHR, and STG — positively characterised by Treat (V-test = 3.52), Guests (2.86), Gift (2.18), PubHouse (2.15), and Achievement (2.05), and under-represented by Rugby (-7.07), CampingFishing (-3.34), and ThirstQ (-2.02). This cluster groups beverages more associated with social or treat-related contexts and less with sports and outdoor contexts.
Cluster 3 (green): SSA alone — positively characterised by Gift (V-test = 6.43), FineDinning (6.09), Treat (4.53), Achievement (3.71), and Guests (2.72), and negatively by Rugby (-4.29), ThirstQ (-3.63), Work (-3.01), CampingFishing (-2.88), TV (-2.80), and Party (-2.39). The profile of SSA is singular enough to form a cluster on its own.



4.7.5 Synthetic interpretation
This example clearly shows the value of the function. It does not merely show that an item is often checked: it shows for which stimuli it is truly characteristic, how the stimuli are globally opposed, and which main profiles emerge from the set of responses. Here, the major opposition — captured at 85.59% by the first dimension — contrasts beverages associated with sports and outdoor contexts (Rugby, CampingFishing) with beverages perceived as more sophisticated (Gift, FineDinning, Treat). SSA is a special case, with a profile singular enough to form a cluster on its own.

What we take away from this example: CATA analysis makes it possible to move from simple checking frequencies to a structured reading of the oppositions between stimuli and the main profiles that emerge from them.

4.9 Practical tips

Start with Significance threshold (%) = 5%; increase to 10% if the description tables are too empty.
Always check the contingency table before interpreting the graphs.
At least three CATA terms and three observed stimuli are required to construct the two-dimensional factor map.
A negative V-test is just as informative as a positive V-test: it indicates that a term is checked significantly less often for a stimulus than for the others.
Do not overinterpret the absence of a stimulus from the descriptive table: it may simply have a profile close to the mean profile.
Classification is automatic by default (Number of clusters = -1), but you can impose a number of groups; always assess its relevance by cross-reading the map and the cluster description.
Read the correspondence map together with the description table: the map gives an overview, while the table provides the details.
CATA columns must contain only 0 and 1 and must not contain missing values; a missing value is not treated as an unchecked response.

title: 5  JAR Data — Defect and Penalty Analysis
text:
5.1 Introduction
This analysis is designed for JAR (Just About Right) data, in which subjects evaluate a sensory attribute relative to an ideal level, for example too little / just about right / too much. It identifies deviations from the JAR level, estimates their frequency, and studies their relationship with liking.
SEDA provides two complementary penalty views. The first is a global view, based on SensoMineR::JAR, which estimates the importance of defects across the whole product space. The second is a classical product-specific analysis, which compares, for a given product, the liking of consumers who rate an attribute JAR with that of consumers who rate it below or above JAR.
Why not use a simple mean liking score?
A mean liking score by product does not show which sensory deviations are associated with a decrease in liking. Likewise, the frequency of JAR responses alone does not indicate whether a frequent defect is actually penalising. The value of the analysis is therefore to combine three different pieces of information: defect frequency, size of the liking loss, and statistical uncertainty around that loss.

text:
5.2 Understanding what happens under the hood

5.2.1 Checking and grouping the JAR coding
The value entered in Coding of the JAR level must exactly match the category representing the ideal level in every selected JAR attribute. The default value is jar.
For the classical product-specific analysis, SEDA then groups the other categories into two directions:

Below JAR;
Above JAR.

This grouping uses the expressions defined in Below-JAR keywords and Above-JAR keywords. The first output to inspect is therefore JAR Coding Used for the Classical Penalty Analysis. A level shown as Unclassified should be resolved before interpreting the classical analysis; otherwise, the corresponding attribute is excluded from that part of the analysis.


5.2.2 Distribution of JAR responses
SEDA calculates, for each product and attribute, the percentages of consumers Below JAR, JAR, and Above JAR. This output describes how frequent the deviations are, but does not yet indicate whether they reduce liking.


5.2.3 Global multidimensional penalties
SensoMineR::JAR estimates penalties using all products simultaneously. In SEDA, they are presented as Mean drop values: a positive value means that the defect is associated with a loss of liking across the global product space.
These coefficients are global and are not product-specific estimates. SEDA then combines them with the frequency of each defect in each product in Global Defects Applied to Each Product.
A row receives Priority = Yes when three conditions are met:

the percentage of consumers reaches Consumer threshold (%);
the Global mean drop reaches Mean-drop threshold;
the global penalty p-value is below 0.05.

The two interface thresholds are therefore practical decision aids, not substitutes for the p-value.


5.2.4 Classical product-specific penalty analysis
SEDA also calculates, separately for each product, attribute, and direction (Below JAR or Above JAR):
Mean drop = Mean liking JAR − Mean liking non-JAR
A positive value therefore means that consumers perceiving the deviation give a lower mean liking score than consumers rating the attribute JAR.
For each comparison, SEDA reports:

the percentage of consumers concerned;
mean liking in the JAR group;
mean liking in the non-JAR group;
Mean drop;
its 95% confidence interval;
the p-value.

This analysis is genuinely product-specific and complements the global penalty view.


5.2.5 Multivariate synthesis of defects
Finally, SEDA constructs a products × non-JAR categories frequency table, describes it with descfreq(), and performs a correspondence analysis.
The product description deliberately uses a permissive exploratory threshold (proba = 0.5). It is intended to reveal the categories structuring the space and should not be interpreted as a conventional 5% significance filter.
The correspondence map summarises the product × defect structure. As in the CATA chapter, products and defects should be interpreted relative to the factor dimensions; a direct row-to-column distance is not an ordinary Euclidean distance. Proximity on this map is not, by itself, evidence of a liking penalty.

text:
5.4 Interface guide
The analysis appears in SEDA > Fixed List of Attributes > Analysis of JAR Data. The interface includes four variable drop zones, an Instructions and R Code section, the Coding of the JAR level field, and a Classical Penalty Analysis section.

5.4.1 Variables to complete

5.4.1.1 Stimulus Effect
Role: identifies the products to analyse. Impact on the computation: this variable defines the products used in both global and product-specific analyses. Practical tip: use short, explicit labels.


5.4.1.2 Subject Effect
Role: identifies the subjects. Impact on the computation: this variable is used by the global JAR analysis and structures individual observations. Practical tip: ensure that each subject keeps the same identifier throughout the dataset.


5.4.1.3 Liking Variable
Role: contains the liking score used to calculate penalties. Impact on the computation: all liking losses are expressed in the units of this variable. Practical tip: use the same liking scale for all products.


5.4.1.4 Sensory Attributes
Role: groups the JAR variables. Impact on the computation: each variable is used in the global, product-specific, and multivariate analyses. Practical tip: variables must be nominal, even when their categories conceptually follow an order such as too little / JAR / too much.



5.4.2 Instructions and R Code

5.4.2.1 Read me before running
Role: displays integrated help. Impact on the computation: none. It is enabled by default.


5.4.2.2 R code
Role: displays the R script reproducing the analysis. Impact on the computation: none. Enable it to continue the analysis in the Rj Editor. It is disabled by default.



5.4.3 Coding of the JAR level
Role: gives the exact label of the JAR category. Impact on the computation: this category is used as the reference in all analyses. Practical tip: the default is jar; match the label in the data exactly.


5.4.4 Classical Penalty Analysis

5.4.4.1 Consumer threshold (%)
Role: defines the percentage of consumers above which a defect is considered frequent enough for an operational reading. Default: 20%. Important: this is a decision aid, not a significance threshold.


5.4.4.2 Mean-drop threshold
Role: defines the liking loss above which an effect is considered large enough for an operational reading. Default: 1. Important: this threshold concerns effect size, not statistical uncertainty.


5.4.4.3 Below-JAR keywords
Role: defines the words or expressions used to recognise categories below the JAR level. The default is too low|not enough|too weak|plain|low.


5.4.4.4 Above-JAR keywords
Role: defines the words or expressions used to recognise categories above the JAR level. The default is too high|too much|too strong|vivid|high.
Practical tip: always start by checking JAR Coding Used for the Classical Penalty Analysis. If a category is Unclassified, adapt the keywords before interpreting product-specific results.

title: 5  JAR Data — Defect and Penalty Analysis
text:
5.5 Step-by-step procedure

Open the dataset in jamovi.
Check that Stimulus Effect and Subject Effect are categorical, Liking Variable is numeric, and JAR attributes are nominal.
Open SEDA > Fixed List of Attributes > Analysis of JAR Data.
Fill Stimulus Effect, Subject Effect, Liking Variable, and Sensory Attributes.
Check Coding of the JAR level.
Leave Consumer threshold (%) = 20 and Mean-drop threshold = 1 for a first reading.
Check Below-JAR keywords and Above-JAR keywords.
Read JAR Coding Used for the Classical Penalty Analysis and resolve any Unclassified category.
Read Distribution of JAR Responses by Product and Attribute.
Examine Global Multidimensional Penalties (All Products) and then Global Defects Applied to Each Product.
Use Global Penalty Context for Each Product to see which products are exposed to globally important defects.
Then read Product-Specific Classical Penalty Analysis and the Product-Specific Penalty Plots.
Finish with Description of the Products According to Defects, Representation of the Products and the Defects, and Frequency Table Used for the Correspondence Analysis.
Cross-read frequency, mean-drop magnitude, and statistical uncertainty before retaining a product-optimisation lever.

title: 5  JAR Data — Defect and Penalty Analysis
text:
5.6 Interpretation of results

5.6.1 JAR Coding Used for the Classical Penalty Analysis
This table is the essential preliminary check. For each attribute and original response level, it shows whether SEDA uses it as Below JAR, JAR, Above JAR, or Unclassified.
An Unclassified category should not be ignored: the corresponding attribute is excluded from the classical product-specific analysis until its coding is resolved.


5.6.2 Distribution of JAR Responses by Product and Attribute
For each product and attribute, this table reports:

Below JAR (%);
JAR (%);
Above JAR (%);
N.

It answers the question: how many consumers actually perceive the deviation? It does not measure its impact on liking.


5.6.3 Global Multidimensional Penalties (All Products)
This table contains the coefficients from SensoMineR::JAR:



Column
Interpretation




Defect
Non-JAR category


Mean drop
Global liking loss associated with the defect


Std. Error
Estimation uncertainty


p
Associated statistical evidence



Mean drop is presented so that a positive value corresponds to a loss of liking.

Point of vigilance: these coefficients are estimated across all products. They should not be described as product-specific penalties.



5.6.4 Global Defects Applied to Each Product
This table combines the local frequency of a defect in each product with its Global mean drop.







Column
Interpretation




Consumers (%)
Defect frequency in the product


Global mean drop
Globally estimated mean drop


p
Global penalty p-value


Priority
Yes if frequency, mean drop, and p-value meet the criteria



With the default settings, Priority = Yes therefore means at least 20% of consumers concerned, a mean drop of at least 1, and p < .05.


5.6.5 Global Penalty Context for Each Product
These graphs provide the native SensoMineR visualisation of the global penalty in the context of each product. They help identify products exposed to globally important defects, but the y-coordinate does not thereby become a product-specific penalty.


5.6.6 Product-Specific Classical Penalty Analysis
This table answers a different question: for this specific product, do consumers perceiving the attribute as non-JAR like the product less than consumers rating it JAR?



Column
Interpretation




Product
Product concerned


Attribute
JAR attribute


Direction
Below JAR or Above JAR


Consumers (%)
Percentage of consumers in that direction


Mean liking JAR
Mean liking in the JAR group


Mean liking non-JAR
Mean liking in the relevant non-JAR group


Mean drop
Mean liking JAR − Mean liking non-JAR


CI 95% low / high
95% confidence interval for the mean drop


p
Test p-value



A positive Mean drop indicates a liking loss associated with the deviation for that product.


5.6.7 Product-Specific Penalty Plots
For each product:

the x-axis represents Consumers concerned (%);
the y-axis represents Mean drop in liking;
the vertical dashed line corresponds to the Consumer threshold;
the horizontal dashed line corresponds to the Mean-drop threshold;
symbols distinguish Below JAR from Above JAR;
* indicates p < .05;
vertical intervals show the 95% confidence interval.

A defect in the high-frequency / high-mean-drop region may be an operational lever, but confidence intervals and p-values should remain part of the decision.


5.6.8 Description of the Products According to Defects
This table describes the non-JAR categories structuring each product profile. It deliberately uses a very permissive exploratory threshold in this multivariate synthesis. A category displayed with p > .05 is therefore not “significant at 5%”; it is retained to help interpret the structure of the space.


5.6.9 Representation of the Products and the Defects
This map comes from correspondence analysis of the products × defects table. Two nearby products have similar defect profiles. For product-to-defect relationships, interpret directions and factor dimensions rather than a direct row-to-column distance.
This map describes the structure of defects; it is not a test of liking penalty.


5.6.10 Frequency Table Used for the Correspondence Analysis
This table contains the products × non-JAR-category frequencies used by descfreq() and correspondence analysis. It is a useful audit output for understanding exactly which aggregated data feed the multivariate synthesis.
