title: 5  JAR Data — Defect and Penalty Analysis
text:
5.7 Example: the milkshake dataset
The milkshake dataset contains three milkshakes, 284, 859, and 972, evaluated by 47 consumers using several JAR attributes related to color, fluidity, odors, sweetness, acidity, texture, and taste. To load the dataset, open jamovi, click the icon in the top left corner, then Open → Data Library → SEDA.
This example is especially useful because it shows that the global and product-specific views can lead to complementary diagnoses.

5.7.1 Example settings







Option
Value




Stimulus Effect
Product


Subject Effect
Panelist


Liking Variable
Liking


Sensory Attributes
all JAR variables from Color to Taste_Van


Coding of the JAR level
jar


Consumer threshold (%)
20


Mean-drop threshold
1


Below-JAR keywords
too low|not enough|too weak|plain|low


Above-JAR keywords
too high|too much|too strong|vivid|high|too_fluid



The final term added to Above-JAR keywords correctly classifies Too_fluid as Above JAR. SEDA accepts both Too_fluid and too fluid: original labels and their normalised forms are recognised.


5.7.2 Check the JAR coding first
The JAR Coding Used for the Classical Penalty Analysis table confirms that all response levels used in this example are classified as Below JAR, JAR, or Above JAR. For Fluidity, Not_enough_fluid is classified as Below JAR and Too_fluid as Above JAR.
This check matters because the classical product-specific analysis can only be interpreted when the non-JAR categories of the attribute are correctly grouped.


5.7.3 Distribution of JAR responses
The Distribution of JAR Responses by Product and Attribute table identifies the most frequent deviations.
For 284, Below JAR responses are particularly frequent for Odor_Van (59.57%), Texture (57.45%), and Odor_Int (53.19%), while 46.81% of consumers rate Fluidity Above JAR.
For 859, two deviations dominate: 80.85% of consumers are Below JAR for Texture and 70.21% are Above JAR for Fluidity.
For 972, 55.32% are Below JAR for Odor_Int, 42.55% are Above JAR for Sweetness, and 38.30% are Above JAR for Fluidity.
These percentages describe prevalence. They do not by themselves show that the deviations reduce liking.


5.7.4 Global multidimensional penalties
In Global Multidimensional Penalties (All Products), only one defect is significant at the 5% level: Too_much_odor_fruit, with Mean drop = 2.68 and p = 0.018.
Several other effects have notable mean drops without reaching the 5% threshold, for example Too_much_acidity (4.02, p = 0.082), Too_much_texture (1.78, p = 0.089), and Not_enough_acidity (1.03, p = 0.087).
In SEDA, a positive Mean drop represents a loss of liking.


5.7.5 Global Defects Applied to Each Product
With Consumer threshold = 20% and Mean-drop threshold = 1, no row receives Priority = Yes.
Too_much_odor_fruit is the only globally significant defect, but it concerns only 6.38% of consumers for 284, 4.26% for 859, and 4.26% for 972. It is therefore statistically associated with a liking loss across the global product space, but it is too rare within each product to exceed the practical 20% threshold.
Conversely, Too_fluid is very frequent — 46.81% for 284, 70.21% for 859, and 38.30% for 972 — but its Global mean drop = 0.45 with p = 0.275. High prevalence and global penalty therefore do not necessarily coincide.


5.7.6 Classical product-specific penalties
The Product-Specific Classical Penalty Analysis provides a directly local view.
For 284, several deviations are associated with a significant liking loss:

Odor_Fruit — Below JAR: 46.81% of consumers, Mean drop = 1.00, 95% CI [0.04, 1.96], p = 0.042;
Odor_Fruit — Above JAR: 6.38%, Mean drop = 2.27, 95% CI [0.47, 4.08], p = 0.016;
Sweetness — Below JAR: 21.28%, Mean drop = 1.22, 95% CI [0.04, 2.40], p = 0.044;
Texture — Below JAR: 57.45%, Mean drop = 1.06, 95% CI [0.10, 2.02], p = 0.032.

For Fluidity — Above JAR, 46.81% of consumers are concerned, but Mean drop is only 0.69 with p = 0.182. The deviation is therefore frequent without being clearly penalising for 284.
For 859, Fluidity — Above JAR gives a particularly instructive result: 70.21% of consumers are concerned, but Mean drop is only 0.87, p = 0.298. Likewise, Texture — Below JAR concerns 80.85% of consumers but has Mean drop = 0.98, p = 0.272. These two deviations are extremely frequent without a clearly established hedonic impact in the product-specific analysis.
The two significant effects for 859 instead concern very small groups:

Odor_Fruit — Above JAR: 4.26%, Mean drop = 3.55, p = 0.013;
Taste_Fruit — Above JAR: 6.38%, Mean drop = 2.83, p = 0.019.

The effects are large but rare, which limits their operational priority.
For 972, Fluidity — Above JAR concerns 38.30% of consumers with Mean drop = 1.06 and p = 0.080: the signal is compatible with a liking loss but remains insufficient to conclude at the 5% level.
Two other effects are significant:

Color — Above JAR: 6.38%, Mean drop = 2.74, p = 0.009;
Taste_Van — Above JAR: 21.28%, Mean drop = 1.57, 95% CI [0.19, 2.95], p = 0.028.

The second is especially useful because it combines frequency above 20%, mean drop above 1, and p < .05. Taste_Van — Above JAR is therefore the clearest product-specific optimisation lever for 972.


5.7.7 What the product-specific plots show
The Product-Specific Penalty Plots make this logic visible: the vertical line marks 20% of consumers and the horizontal line marks a mean drop of 1.
For 284, several significant points lie in or near the upper-right region, especially lack of texture, sweetness, and fruity odor.
For 859, Fluidity — Above JAR and Texture — Below JAR lie far to the right of the graph, meaning that they are very frequent, but remain below or around the mean-drop threshold and are not significant. The two significant effects instead have large mean drops but lie far to the left because they concern few consumers.
For 972, Taste_Van — Above JAR combines frequency, effect size, and statistical evidence, whereas Fluidity — Above JAR is a more uncertain signal.
These plots show why frequency, effect size, and uncertainty should be considered together.


5.7.8 Multivariate synthesis of defects
The Description of the Products According to Defects table uses the exploratory threshold proba = 0.5. The displayed rows should therefore not all be described as “significant at 5%”.
Product 859 is mainly oriented toward Texture = Not_enough_texture (V-test = 1.92, p = 0.055) and Fluidity = Too_fluid (1.75, p = 0.080), while Color = A_little_plain (-2.05, p = 0.040) and Odor_Van = Not_enough_odor_van (-1.97, p = 0.049) are under-represented.
Product 972 is notably oriented toward Sweetness = Too_much_sweetness (V-test = 1.71, p = 0.087), while Texture = Not_enough_texture is under-represented (V-test = -1.80, p = 0.072).
Product 284 shows a less marked structure; its strongest positive category is Color = A_little_plain (V-test = 1.32, p = 0.187).


5.7.9 Representation of the Products and the Defects
The correspondence analysis is entirely summarised by the two available dimensions: Dim. 1 = 74.78% and Dim. 2 = 25.22%.
Dim. 1 mainly opposes 859 and 972, while 284 occupies a more intermediate position. The map summarises the non-JAR profile structure, but product-to-defect relationships should be interpreted relative to the factor dimensions rather than from simple row-to-column proximity.


5.7.10 Synthetic interpretation
The example mainly shows that the different pieces of JAR information are not redundant.
The global view identifies Too_much_odor_fruit as the only defect clearly associated with a liking loss across the whole product space, but this defect is too rare within each product to become a priority under the 20% threshold.
The product-specific view instead shows that extremely frequent deviations may be weakly or non-penalising: this is the case for Too_fluid and Not_enough_texture for 859. It also reveals local levers, including several deviations for 284 and especially Taste_Van — Above JAR for 972.

What we take away from this example: useful JAR analysis is not about finding “the most penalising defect”. It distinguishes what is frequent, what is globally penalising, what is specifically penalising for a product, and what combines enough frequency, effect size, and statistical evidence to become an optimisation priority.

title: 5  JAR Data — Defect and Penalty Analysis
text:
5.9 Practical tips

Always inspect JAR Coding Used for the Classical Penalty Analysis before interpreting product-specific penalties.
JAR variables must be defined as Nominal in jamovi and must contain exactly the level specified in Coding of the JAR level.
An Unclassified category indicates a Below/Above JAR grouping problem: adapt the keyword patterns before interpreting the classical analysis.
Do not confuse the two views: Global Multidimensional Penalties describes the whole product space, whereas Product-Specific Classical Penalty Analysis answers the question separately for each product.
A positive Mean drop indicates a liking loss. Interpret its magnitude together with the percentage of consumers concerned, the confidence interval, and the p-value.
Consumer threshold (%) and Mean-drop threshold are practical decision thresholds, not significance thresholds.
A frequent defect is not necessarily penalising; a strongly penalising but very rare defect is not necessarily a priority.
Use the correspondence-analysis map to understand the structure of defect profiles, not to conclude that a defect affects liking.

title: 5  JAR Data — Defect and Penalty Analysis
text:
5.10 In summary
Use this analysis when JAR responses are available together with a liking measure and the objective is to identify deviations from the ideal level that may guide product optimisation.
SEDA first checks the JAR coding, then describes the Below/JAR/Above response frequencies, and provides two complementary views: a global penalty analysis across the whole product space and a classical product-specific penalty analysis. The multivariate correspondence-analysis synthesis completes these diagnostics by showing how products are structured according to their non-JAR categories.
Read the coding and distributions first, then the global penalties, next the product-specific penalties, and finish with the factorial synthesis.
The main point is that an optimisation priority should not rely on a single cutoff: it should combine defect frequency, mean-drop magnitude, and statistical uncertainty.

title: 6  Napping Data — Consensus Representation
text:
6.1 Introduction
This analysis is designed for Napping (projective mapping) data, in which each subject positions a set of stimuli in a two-dimensional space according to their perceived similarities and differences. It makes it possible to construct a consensus representation of the stimuli from several individual maps and, if desired, to group the stimuli into clusters. The function relies on a Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) to merge the different pairs of coordinates into a single space.
Why not use a standard alternative?
A PCA applied directly to all coordinate columns would account for relationships among the variables, but would ignore their grouping by subject. In Napping, the data are naturally organised as X/Y pairs provided by each subject. Here, each pair is treated as a group in the MFA, which makes it possible to construct a more suitable compromise between the different individual maps. This MFA uses type = "c" in FactoMineR: the coordinates are centred but not standardised, preserving the geometry and relative scale of each Napping sheet rather than forcing X and Y to have the same variance.
crumbs: 6  Napping Data — Consensus Representation

title: 6  Napping Data — Consensus Representation
section: 6.2 Understanding what happens under the hood
text:
6.2 Understanding what happens under the hood

6.2.1 The data are read as pairs of coordinates
The function expects in Active (X,Y) Coordinate Pairs a set of numeric columns organised as consecutive pairs: X then Y for a first subject, X then Y for a second subject, and so on. The same principle applies to Supplementary (X,Y) Coordinate Pairs. If the number of columns is odd in either block, the analysis is rejected. The active block must contain at least 4 columns, that is, 2 pairs. The same coordinate cannot be selected as both active and supplementary.


6.2.2 An MFA on groups of size 2, without standardisation
The core of the analysis is an MFA. Each X/Y pair in Active (X,Y) Coordinate Pairs is treated as a group of two quantitative variables. The MFA constructs a common space that summarises the information carried by all subjects while balancing the contribution of the groups. With type = "c", the coordinates are centred but not standardised, preserving the relative scale of the two coordinates in each individual configuration.


6.2.3 The role of supplementary coordinates
If you provide variables in Supplementary (X,Y) Coordinate Pairs, they are projected as supplementary groups in the MFA. They do not participate in the construction of the axes, but make it possible to locate other subjects in the same space.


6.2.4 Automatic description of the dimensions
Once the MFA has been computed, the function produces an automatic description of the dimensions filtered by Significance threshold (%) and Number of dimensions. This output helps understand which variables are most strongly linked to the first axes.


6.2.5 Saving dimensions and clustering
The Number of dimensions to save/use for clustering field determines how many first dimensions are saved in Coordinates and used for clustering. If fewer dimensions are available than requested, SEDA uses those that can actually be computed. If you activate Representation of the clusters or request Cluster variable, the function runs an HCPC on these retained dimensions. By default, clustering uses the first 5 dimensions, and Number of clusters = -1 lets FactoMineR choose the number of clusters automatically. The analysis appears in SEDA > Free Perception > Analysis of Napping Data. The interface includes three variable drop zones, an Instructions and R Code section, followed by the Graphic Options, Numerical Indicators, and Clustering menus.

6.4.1 Variables to complete

6.4.1.1 Stimuli Labels
Role: provides the names of the stimuli in the outputs. Impact on the computation: this variable does not modify the MFA itself, but determines the labels displayed in the graphs and the names associated with the saved coordinates. Practical tip: use short and unique labels; otherwise, the maps quickly become difficult to read.


6.4.1.2 Active (X,Y) Coordinate Pairs
Role: groups together the active coordinates used to construct the consensus representation. Impact on the computation: each X/Y pair becomes a group in the MFA. The number of columns must be even, and the function requires at least 4 columns. Practical tip: strictly respect the order X, Y, X, Y… to avoid incorrectly organising the groups.


6.4.1.3 Supplementary (X,Y) Coordinate Pairs
Role: adds pairs of coordinates projected as supplementary groups. Impact on the computation: these coordinates do not influence the construction of the axes, but are projected into the MFA space. Practical tip: use this block to project a second panel without modifying the main compromise.



6.4.2 Instructions and R Code

6.4.2.1 Read me before running
Role: displays integrated help in the results. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: leave it checked during the first uses. It is enabled by default.


6.4.2.2 R code
Role: displays the R script corresponding to the analysis in an R Code output. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: enable this option to reproduce the analysis in the Rj Editor. It is disabled by default.



6.4.3 Graphic Options

6.4.3.1 X-axis
Role: chooses the dimension displayed on the horizontal axis. Impact on the computation: it does not modify the MFA, but changes the factor plane displayed in the graphs. Practical tip: start with 1, the default value.


6.4.3.2 Y-axis
Role: chooses the dimension displayed on the vertical axis. Impact on the computation: it does not modify the MFA, but changes the factor plane displayed in the graphs. Practical tip: start with 2, the default value.



6.4.4 Numerical Indicators

6.4.4.1 Significance threshold (%)
Role: sets the significance threshold for the automatic description of the dimensions. Impact on the computation: the stricter the threshold, the more selective the automatic description will be. Practical tip: the default value of 5% is a good starting point.


6.4.4.2 Number of dimensions
Role: determines the number of axes described automatically. Impact on the computation: it controls the dimension description output and also helps determine the number of MFA dimensions computed internally. Practical tip: leave 2 for a first reading.


6.4.4.3 Number of dimensions to save/use for clustering
Role: defines the number of first dimensions to save and use for clustering. Impact on the computation: it determines the columns saved in Coordinates and the dimensions passed to HCPC; if fewer dimensions are available, SEDA uses the maximum that can be computed. Practical tip: the default value of 5 is a good starting point.


6.4.4.4 Coordinates
Role: saves the factorial coordinates of the stimuli in the jamovi data sheet. Impact on the computation: it does not add a new calculation, but saves the results of the MFA. Practical tip: activate this output if you want to reuse the dimensions in other jamovi analyses.



6.4.5 Clustering

6.4.5.1 Representation of the clusters
Role: activates the display of the clustering graph. Impact on the computation: when this option is checked, the function computes the HCPC classification if necessary and displays the map of stimuli according to clusters. Practical tip: leave it unchecked for a first reading, then activate it to complement the consensus map with a group-based reading.


6.4.5.2 Number of clusters
Role: sets the number of clusters to extract. Impact on the computation: with -1, the number of clusters is determined automatically; otherwise, you can impose an integer between 2 and the number of stimuli minus 1. Practical tip: start with -1, then set a number only if you have a clear analytical justification.


6.4.5.3 Cluster variable
Role: saves the cluster membership of each stimulus as a new variable in jamovi. Impact on the computation: it does not add a new calculation, but saves the results of the classification. Practical tip: useful if you then want to cross the clusters with other variables in jamovi.

6.6 Interpretation of results

6.6.1 Representation of the Stimuli
This is the important result of the function. It represents the stimuli in the consensus factor space constructed by the MFA. Two close stimuli were positioned similarly by the set of subjects; two distant stimuli are perceived as more different. The percentage displayed on each axis indicates the share of variance explained by the corresponding dimension.

Point of vigilance: the stimulus map shows a perceptual structure, but it is not always sufficient to name the axes. Adding supplementary information, such as verbalisation, can greatly help interpretation.



6.6.2 Representation of the Subjects
This map represents the X/Y coordinate groups — that is, the subjects’ individual configurations — in the factor space. It shows how each Napping sheet relates to the dimensions of the compromise.







Element

6.6.5 Representation of the Stimuli According to Clusters (available if “Representation of the clusters” is activated)

6.7 Example: the perfumes_napping dataset
The perfumes_napping dataset describes 12 perfumes positioned on a sheet (with dimensions 60 by 40) by 60 subjects, that is, 120 coordinate columns (one X/Y pair per subject). It is used to illustrate the function outputs. The numerical values and graphics discussed below come directly from the analysis results. To load this dataset, open jamovi, click the icon in the top left corner, the three stacked lines, then Open → Data Library → SEDA.

6.7.2 Analysis of the Representation of the Stimuli graph
The map reveals a fairly clear perceptual structure on the Dim. 1 (25.07%) / Dim. 2 (18.03%) plane. On the horizontal axis, Aromatics Elixir and Shalimar are clearly located on the right (positive coordinates on Dim. 1), whereas J’adore EP, J’adore ET, Coco Mademoiselle, Cinéma, Pleasures, and Pure Poison are located on the left. Chanel N5 differs from this right-hand group by a low position on the second dimension (strongly negative value on Dim. 2), which slightly isolates it from the Shalimar / Aromatics Elixir pair. On the vertical axis, Angel, Lolita Lempicka, and L’instant are clearly located above the centre, forming a coherent perceptual group at the top of the plane.


6.7.3 Analysis of the Representation of the Subjects graph
The subject map represents the 60 coordinate groups, S1 to S60. Groups far from the origin on Dim. 1, such as S1 or S20, are strongly related to the first common dimension. Groups such as S4 or S30, located higher on Dim. 2, are more strongly related to the second. The many groups close to the origin are less strongly associated with the two displayed dimensions. This map therefore describes the relationship between individual configurations and the compromise; it is not, by itself, a numerical index of consensus.


6.7.4 Analysis of the Eigenvalue Decomposition table
The first two dimensions explain 43.09% of the total variance (Dim. 1: 25.07%, Dim. 2: 18.03%). The 1/2 plane therefore provides a useful first summary, but more than half of the variability lies beyond this plane. The following dimensions remain non-negligible (Dim. 3: 12.31%, Dim. 4: 9.58%, Dim. 5: 7.96%), which justifies examining other factor planes when needed.


6.7.5 Analysis of the Automatic Description of the Dimensions table
The Automatic Description of the Dimensions output identifies the X/Y coordinates most correlated with each axis. For Dim. 1, the strongest positive correlations are X20 (r = 0.93), X1 (r = 0.92), and Y21 (r = 0.90). At the opposite end, Y48 (r = -0.91) and X42 (r = -0.85) have the strongest negative correlations. These results identify which directions of the individual configurations are most aligned with, or opposed to, the first compromise dimension. They do not by themselves provide a sensory meaning for the axis.


6.7.6 Analysis of the Representation of the Stimuli According to Clusters graph
With Number of dimensions to save/use for clustering = 5, the retained MFA dimensions account for 72.95% of the total inertia. The HCPC map therefore expresses Dim. 1 and Dim. 2 relative to this five-dimensional space: approximately 34.37% and 24.72%, rather than 25.07% and 18.03% on the full MFA map.
With Number of clusters = -1, the automatic classification retains three clusters:

Cluster 1 (black): Coco Mademoiselle, J’adore EP, J’adore ET, Cinéma, Pleasures, and Pure Poison;
Cluster 2 (red): Angel, Lolita Lempicka, and L’instant;
Cluster 3 (green): Shalimar, Aromatics Elixir, and Chanel N5.

On the 1/2 plane, the first group lies mainly on the left, the second at the top, and the third on the right and lower part of the map. However, the classification is calculated from the first five retained dimensions, not only from this plane. Without external sensory information or verbalisation, qualities such as “floral”, “light”, or “intense” should not be assigned automatically to these clusters.


6.7.7 Synthetic interpretation
This example clearly shows the value of the function. It does not only provide an average map of the perfumes: it constructs a consensus space, shows how the individual configurations relate to its dimensions, and identifies which groups of perfumes emerge from the classification. The three clusters are clear in this example, but their sensory interpretation would require additional information.

What we take away from this example: Napping analysis transforms a set of individual maps into a consensus representation, then makes it possible to examine the relationships between individual configurations and common dimensions as well as the groups of stimuli.

6.8 From jamovi to the Rj Editor

title: 6  Napping Data — Consensus Representation
text:
6.10 In summary
This analysis constructs a consensus map of the stimuli from Napping data by combining the individual maps through a centred but non-standardised MFA that balances the contribution of the groups. It represents the structure of the stimuli and the relationship between individual configurations and the common dimensions, and can be complemented by an HCPC clustering of the stimuli on the retained dimensions. Its main value is to transform a set of individual maps into a common representation of perceptual proximities, without requiring a predefined list of attributes.

title: 7  Sorting Data — Analysis of Categorisation
text:
7.1 Introduction
This analysis is designed for free sorting (sorting task) data, in which each subject groups stimuli into categories according to their own perception. It makes it possible to obtain a multivariate representation of the stimuli from the categorisations provided by the subjects, and, if needed, an automatic classification of the stimuli into groups. When the groups have been verbalised, the function also provides a textual description of the stimuli based on the words used to name these groups.
Why not use a standard alternative?
A classical approach consists of transforming the sorting data into a similarity matrix between stimuli, then applying a projection method such as MDS. This strategy is useful, but it removes part of the individual information carried by each subject. Here, the function directly analyses the columns in Active Subjects as qualitative variables and applies a Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), which preserves more of the structure of individual responses and makes it possible to represent stimuli and categories simultaneously in the same space.

title: 7  Sorting Data — Analysis of Categorisation
section: 7.2 Understanding what happens under the hood
text:
7.2 Understanding what happens under the hood

7.2.1 The stimuli are the individuals in the analysis
The function reads the columns placed in Active Subjects as categorical variables. Each row corresponds to a stimulus, and each column indicates in which group a subject placed this stimulus. If Stimuli Labels is completed, this variable is used to name the stimuli in the outputs; otherwise, the function uses row numbers.


7.2.2 An MCA on the categorisations provided by the subjects
The core of the function is an MCA applied to the columns in Active Subjects. In this framework, two stimuli are close when their sorting profiles are similar across the active subjects. The columns placed in Supplementary Subjects, if any, are projected as supplementary qualitative variables: they appear in the factor space, but do not participate in the construction of the axes.


7.2.3 The role of Ventilation level (%)
The Ventilation level (%) parameter is passed to FactoMineR’s MCA. Categories whose frequency falls below the threshold are ventilated before the MCA: the affected stimuli are randomly reassigned to other observed categories of the same variable. This limits the influence of extremely rare categories but can introduce slight variation between runs. The default value is 5%; a value of 0% disables ventilation.


7.2.4 Textual description of the stimuli
The function constructs a stimuli × words correspondence table from the group labels, then applies a frequency description procedure. This part is used to identify, for each stimulus, the most characteristic words among the labels used by the subjects. It becomes particularly useful when the groups have been named with interpretable sensory terms.


7.2.5 Automatic description of the dimensions and clustering
Once the MCA has been computed, the function produces an automatic description of the dimensions according to Significance threshold (%) and Number of dimensions. If you activate Representation of the clusters, the function applies HCPC to the stimulus coordinates on the retained components. By default, clustering is based on the first 5 components, and Number of clusters = -1 lets HCPC choose the number of groups automatically. The percentages displayed on the HCPC map refer to this retained space and may therefore differ from those on the full MCA map.

7.4 Interface guide
The analysis appears in SEDA > Free Perception > Analysis of Sorting Data. The interface includes three variable drop zones, the Instructions and R Code section, and then the Random Assignment for Rare Categories, Graphic Options, Numerical Indicators, and Clustering sections.

7.4.1 Variables to complete

7.4.1.1 Stimuli Labels
Role: provides the names of the stimuli in the outputs. Impact on the computation: it does not modify the MCA, but determines the labels displayed in the graphs and the names associated with the saved coordinates. Practical tip: use short and unique labels; otherwise, the maps become difficult to read.


7.4.1.2 Active Subjects
Role: groups together the sorting variables that construct the factor space, one per subject. Impact on the computation: these are the active variables of the MCA. Clustering then uses the stimulus coordinates produced by this MCA. At least two variables are required. Practical tip: check that each column is categorical in jamovi.


7.4.1.3 Supplementary Subjects
Role: groups together variables projected as supplementary qualitative variables. Impact on the computation: they do not influence the construction of the axes, but their position in the space can help interpretation. Practical tip: useful for projecting a second group of subjects without modifying the main result.



7.4.2 Instructions and R Code

7.4.2.1 Read me before running
Role: displays integrated help in the results. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: leave it checked during the first uses. It is enabled by default.


7.4.2.2 R code
Role: displays the R script corresponding to the current analysis. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: check this option if you want to reproduce the analysis in the Rj Editor; it is disabled by default.



7.4.3 Random Assignment for Rare Categories: Ventilation level (%)
Role: sets the threshold below which a category is ventilated before the MCA. Impact on the computation: stimuli belonging to a rare category are randomly reassigned to other observed categories of the same variable. The default value is 5%. Practical tip: leave 5% for a first trial; use 0% if you want to keep rare categories without ventilation.


7.4.4 Graphic Options (collapsed by default)

7.4.4.1 X-axis and Y-axis
Role: choose the dimensions displayed on the horizontal and vertical axes. Impact on the computation: they do not modify the MCA, but change the displayed factor plane. Practical tip: start with X-axis = 1 and Y-axis = 2, the default values.


7.4.4.2 Active categories
Role: controls the display of active categories on the category map. Impact on the computation: no effect on the MCA; it only affects visibility in the graph. Practical tip: leave it checked at first. Uncheck it if the map is too crowded.


7.4.4.3 Selection of categories
Role: filters the displayed categories according to a quality-of-representation criterion. Impact on the computation: no effect on the MCA; it only affects display. Practical tip: the default value cos2 10 is a good compromise for lightening the map without losing the best-represented categories.


7.4.4.4 Supplementary categories
Role: controls the display of categories derived from Supplementary Subjects. Impact on the computation: no effect on the MCA. Practical tip: leave it checked if you use supplementary variables and want to compare them visually with the active categories.



7.4.5 Numerical Indicators (collapsed by default)

7.4.5.1 Significance threshold (%)
Role: sets the significance threshold for the automatic description of the dimensions. Impact on the computation: the stricter the threshold, the more selective the output. Practical tip: the default value of 5% is well suited to a first reading.


7.4.5.2 Number of dimensions
Role: determines the number of axes described automatically. Impact on the computation: it controls the dimension description output. Practical tip: leave 2 for a first trial.


7.4.5.3 Description of the Stimuli from Sorting Labels — Significance threshold (%)
Role: sets the threshold used for the textual description of the stimuli. Impact on the computation: a stricter threshold produces a shorter description; a broader threshold retains more words. Practical tip: leave 5% at first. If the textual description is too sparse, test a slightly broader threshold.


7.4.5.4 Long-format textual data
Role: displays the intermediate textual dataset in long format. Impact on the computation: it does not add a new calculation; it makes it possible to check how the labels were reorganised before the textual analysis. Practical tip: activate this option if you want to inspect the transformation of the verbal data.


7.4.5.5 Stimulus Table Options — Coordinates, Contributions, Cosine
Role: activate the display of the numerical tables of coordinates, contributions, and cosines for the stimuli. Impact on the computation: no effect on the MCA; they add numerical result tables. Practical tip: disabled by default. Activate them if you want precise values for complementary analyses.


7.4.5.6 Subject Table Options — Coordinates, Contributions, Cosine
Role: same principle for the MCA subjects. Impact on the computation: no effect on the MCA. Practical tip: useful if you want to examine their positions and quality of representation precisely.


7.4.5.7 Number of components (Save)
Role: defines the number of components saved in Coordinates and used for classification. Impact on the computation: HCPC works on the stimulus coordinates in this retained space. Practical tip: the default value of 5 is a useful starting point.


7.4.5.8 Coordinates (Save)
Role: saves the factorial coordinates of the stimuli in the jamovi data sheet. Impact on the computation: no effect on the MCA. Practical tip: activate it if you want to reuse the components in other jamovi analyses.



7.4.6 Clustering (collapsed by default)

7.4.6.1 Representation of the clusters
Role: activates HCPC classification and displays the corresponding graph. Impact on the computation: HCPC uses the first components defined by Number of components. It is unchecked by default. Practical tip: leave it unchecked for a first reading, then activate it to complement the factor map with a group-based reading.


7.4.6.2 Number of clusters
Role: sets the number of clusters to extract. Impact on the computation: with -1, the number is chosen automatically; any positive value imposes that number. Practical tip: start with -1, then set a number only if you have a clear analytical reason.


7.4.6.3 Cluster variable (Save)
Role: saves the cluster membership of each stimulus in the jamovi data sheet. Impact on the computation: it does not add a new calculation, but saves the classification results. Practical tip: useful if you then want to cross the clusters with other variables in jamovi.

7.7.2 Analysis of the Description of the Stimuli table
The table shows that several perfumes have very marked lexical profiles. A few particularly clear readings, with the actual values from the analysis:
Aromatics Elixir is strongly associated with strong (test value 4.08, p < .001; 14.16% of internal occurrences versus 4.65% overall), ammonia (test value 2.26), and spicy (2.18). Conversely, it is clearly under-represented by fruit (test value -2.63), flower (-2.40), and sweet (-2.10): it is the most intense and least floral or sweet perfume in the panel.
Chanel N5 stands out with soap (test value 3.72, p < .001; 7.69% versus 1.61% overall), deodorant (2.06), and unpleasant (1.99), while being under-represented by fruit (-2.47) and flower (-2.21).
Lolita Lempicka is characterised by sweet (test value 3.94, p < .001; 14.55% versus 4.98% overall) and vanilla (2.09), but is under-represented by flower (-2.34).
Pleasures is the perfume most associated with flower (test value 3.46, p < .001; 15.00% versus 5.70% overall) and fresh (2.05), and clearly opposed to strong (-2.46).
Shalimar is characterised by old (test value 2.67, p = 0.008) and sun (2.40), and under-represented by flower (-2.42).
Angel is associated with vanilla (2.23), heady (1.99), and too (1.99), but under-represented by fresh (-2.03) and flower (-2.19).


7.7.3 Analysis of the Representation of the Stimuli graph
The map reveals a readable perceptual structure on the Dim. 1 (15.53%) / Dim. 2 (14.14%) plane. On the right side of the plane, Shalimar, Aromatics Elixir, and Chanel N5 form a group — confirming their strong, spicy, and low-floral profile. On the lower left, J’adore ET, J’adore EP, and Pleasures group together around a floral and fresh profile. At the top, Angel and Lolita Lempicka occupy a clearly distinct position on the second dimension — a vanilla and sweet profile. Cinéma, L’instant, and Coco Mademoiselle form an intermediate central-left area, with profiles that are more difficult to name without the textual description.


7.7.4 Analysis of the Eigenvalue Decomposition table
The first two dimensions explain 29.67% of the total variance (15.53% + 14.14%). This is clearly less concentrated than in a classical PCA: in free sorting, subjects have very different ways of structuring the space, which spreads the information across many dimensions. The 1/2 plane is a useful but partial summary — as confirmed by the following dimensions (Dim. 3: 11.03%, Dim. 4: 9.97%, etc.).


7.7.5 Analysis of the Automatic Description of the Dimensions table
On Dim. 1, the categories most strongly associated with the positive side (right, strong perfumes) are solvent (S52, estimate 1.31), unpleasant (S46, 1.27), spicy (S40, 1.24), very;strong;perfume;woman;old (S15, 1.32), soap;ancient (S48, 1.26), and acid (S54, 1.22). The negative side is associated with flower;fresh (S43, -0.60), fresh;light (S23, -0.81), and flower (S47, -0.68). Dim. 1 therefore clearly opposes strong, spicy, acidic, or unpleasant perfumes to fresh and floral perfumes.
On Dim. 2, the positive side is dominated by vanilla;spicy;hot (S16, 1.51), woman;mature (S7, 1.55), sweet;too;strong (S11, 1.43), teenage;likeable (S51, 1.54), and vanilla;sweet (S34, 1.05). The negative side includes soap (S12, -1.03) and fresh (S10, -0.50). Dim. 2 therefore opposes vanilla, sweet, enveloping perfumes to fresher or soapy profiles.


7.7.6 Analysis of the Representation of the Stimuli According to Clusters graph
With Number of components = 5, HCPC works on the first five MCA dimensions, which together account for 59.59% of the inertia. The classification map therefore displays 26.06% on Dim. 1 and 23.73% on Dim. 2 instead of 15.53% and 14.14% on the MCA map: the percentages are renormalized within the five-dimensional space actually used for clustering.
With Number of clusters = -1, the automatic classification retains six clusters. The labels in parentheses below are supported by the textual and dimension descriptions, not by clustering alone:

a cluster grouping J’adore ET, J’adore EP, and Pleasures (floral, fresh);
a cluster grouping Coco Mademoiselle, L’instant, and Cinéma (intermediate profiles);
a cluster containing only Pure Poison (singular profile);
a cluster grouping Angel and Lolita Lempicka (vanilla, sweet);
a cluster containing only Chanel N5 (soapy, unpleasant);
a cluster grouping Shalimar and Aromatics Elixir (strong, spicy, old).



7.7.7 Synthetic interpretation
This example clearly shows the value of the function. It does not only provide a proximity map between perfumes: it also shows which words subjects associate with each perfume, which oppositions structure the space, and which groups of perfumes emerge from the classification. Cross-reading the description table, the factor map, and the classification makes it possible to name the families more precisely than with the map alone.

What we take away from this example: free sorting analysis makes it possible to link the factorial structure of the categorisations, their verbal interpretation, and the formation of coherent families of stimuli.

This analysis transforms free sorting data into a reading of the stimuli that is simultaneously factorial, textual, and typological. title: 8  Hedonic Data — Preference Mapping
text:
8.1 Introduction
This analysis makes it possible to construct a preference map from two types of information: an already computed two-dimensional representation space, and several Liking Variables corresponding to liking scores. It is used to identify which areas of this space are associated with stronger preference, and to represent the proportion of consumers for whom each region of the plane is predicted to be favourable under the selected threshold. In SEDA, this principle can be used both for external preference mapping (sensory space) and for internal preference mapping (hedonic space), depending on the origin of the two axes used. The analysis can also classify consumers from their liking profiles and produce a preference map for each segment.
Why not use a standard alternative?
A mean liking score by product makes it possible to compare products with one another, but it does not make it possible to relate preferences to an already constructed representation space. Here, the function fits a preference model for each liking variable, then combines these models into a surface indicating the % of consumers associated with each area of the plane. This provides a spatial reading of preferences, which is more informative than a simple table of means.

section: 8.2 Understanding what happens under the hood
text:
8.2 Understanding what happens under the hood

8.2.1 The function does not construct the representation space itself
The function does not calculate the axes of the plane: it expects you to provide one variable for X-axis and one variable for Y-axis. The integrated help text explicitly specifies the recommended workflow: for an external map, these axes may come from a PCA on sensory attributes; for an internal map, they may come from a PCA on hedonic scores. In both cases, the two components must first have been saved in the data, then selected in this module.

How to retrieve dimensions from the MEDA module

Open the MEDA module (menu MEDA > PCA).
Place your variables in the appropriate fields: for an external map, use your sensory attributes; for an internal map, use your hedonic variables.
Expand the Numerical Indicators section, then the Save subsection.
In the Number of components field, enter 2 (or more if you want to explore other planes).
Activate the Coordinates output: jamovi then automatically creates two new columns in your data sheet, named by default Dim. 1 and Dim. 2, containing the coordinates of each stimulus on the first two components.
Then return to SEDA > Hedonic Data > Preference Mapping and place Dim. 1 in X-axis and Dim. 2 in Y-axis.

If your dataset contains the sensory attributes, the hedonic scores, and the stimulus identifiers in the same file — as is the case for the senso_hedo_cocktail dataset — this workflow can be performed entirely in jamovi without any intermediate export or import.



8.2.2 A model is fitted for each liking variable
The function first gathers the two coordinates of the plane and all columns placed in Liking Variables. Each liking column represents one consumer. A separate preference model is fitted for each consumer. The model depends on Regression model:

Quadratic (default): linear effects, quadratic terms, and interaction between the two axes. At least 7 stimuli are required for a non-saturated fit; in practice, more products are preferable.
Vector: linear effects only. At least 4 stimuli are required.
Circular: linear effects with a common radial quadratic curvature. At least 5 stimuli are required.
Elliptical: linear effects and separate quadratic terms on each axis, without interaction. At least 6 stimuli are required.

A simple interpretation is that Vector describes a preference direction; Quadratic allows the most flexible surface; Circular and Elliptical describe local optima under different shape constraints. If the geometry of the two coordinates cannot support the selected model, SEDA asks for a simpler model or a richer product space.


8.2.3 Construction of the preference surface
For each consumer, SEDA fits the selected model to the observed products and predicts liking over a regular grid covering the X-axis / Y-axis plane. Each consumer’s predicted surface is then standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 over the grid.
At each grid location, SEDA counts how many consumers have a standardised predicted value above Preference threshold (SD). This count is converted to a percentage and forms the % of consumers surface.


8.2.4 Preference threshold (SD)
The threshold is expressed in standard deviations of each consumer’s own predicted surface. With the default value 0, a location is considered favourable for a consumer when predicted liking is above that consumer’s average predicted level over the grid. A positive value makes the criterion more selective; a negative value broadens the favourable region. This is a preference criterion, not a statistical significance threshold.


8.2.5 What the final map really represents
The final map does not directly display the observed product-by-product scores. It shows a modelled surface constructed from the individual consumer models. The regions indicate the proportion of consumers for whom each location in the plane exceeds the selected preference threshold. The % of consumers legend should therefore be read as the percentage of consumers for whom a location is predicted to be favourable, not as a mean liking score.


8.2.6 Consumer classification
If Classification of consumers is enabled, classification is computed separately from the preference map. SEDA centres each consumer’s liking profile across stimuli, computes distances between consumers, and applies Ward hierarchical clustering (ward.D2). Centring removes each consumer’s average rating level, so the groups mainly reflect different patterns of preference across products, rather than a simple distinction between consumers who rate high or low overall.
With Number of clusters = -1, SEDA automatically selects a cut from the largest upper-level jump in the hierarchy. A fixed number of groups can also be imposed. Cluster-specific preference maps are then recomputed using the consumers in each group while keeping exactly the same product space, regression model, and preference threshold as the overall map.

8.4.1 Variables to complete

8.4.1.1 Stimuli Labels
Role: provides the names displayed for stimuli on the maps. Impact on the computation: none on the fitted models. Practical tip: use short, complete, and unique labels. If no label variable is supplied, SEDA uses row numbers.


8.4.1.2 X-axis
Role: provides the horizontal coordinate of the stimuli in the representation space. Impact on the computation: directly enters the preference models. Practical tip: typically use the first component saved from a PCA performed in MEDA.


8.4.1.3 Y-axis
Role: provides the vertical coordinate of the stimuli. Impact on the computation: directly enters the models and must come from the same space as X-axis. Practical tip: typically use the second component from the same analysis.


8.4.1.4 Liking Variables
Role: contains individual liking scores, one column per consumer. Impact on the computation: one model is fitted to each column; if classification is enabled, the same profiles are also used to form consumer segments. Practical tip: use individual scores rather than product means.

Role: displays integrated help in the results. Impact on the computation: none. Practical tip: keep it checked during the first uses.


8.4.2.2 R code

8.6 Interpretation of results

8.6.1 Overall Preference Map — main graph
The map shows the space supplied by X-axis and Y-axis, overlaid with the % of consumers surface.







Element
Meaning




Areas toward Color for high preference areas
Regions favourable for a high proportion of consumers according to the selected threshold


Areas toward Color for low preference areas

Intermediate proportions of favourable consumers

Subtitle
Reports the Preference threshold (SD) used



With the default threshold 0, a high region means that a large proportion of consumers have predicted preference above their own average predicted level there. The map therefore represents neither raw mean liking nor a probability in the statistical sense.

Point of vigilance: the surface is modelled over a grid covering the plane. Regions far from observed stimuli involve more extrapolation and should be interpreted cautiously.


Point of vigilance: a visually smooth surface does not guarantee robustness. The number of stimuli, the selected model, and consumer diversity determine how much information is available.



8.6.2 Consumer Cluster Sizes (if Classification of consumers is enabled)
This table gives the number and percentage of consumers in each cluster. It immediately identifies dominant segments and very small groups, which require more cautious interpretation.


8.6.3 Consumer Cluster Membership (if Classification of consumers is enabled)
This table gives the cluster assigned to every consumer. It can be used to reconnect segments with the original liking columns or to characterise the groups in a complementary analysis.


8.6.4 Consumer Cluster Dendrogram (optional)
The dendrogram displays the Ward hierarchical clustering computed from centred liking profiles. Consumers that are close in this hierarchy have similar patterns of preference across products, largely independently of their average rating level.


8.6.5 Preference Maps by Consumer Cluster (optional)
A preference map is recomputed for every cluster using the same product space, Regression model, and Preference threshold (SD) as the overall map. Differences between maps can therefore be interpreted as heterogeneity in preference structure between segments, rather than as changes in the factorial reference space. On a cluster-specific map, the % of consumers is calculated within that cluster: 100% means all consumers in that segment, not all consumers in the full panel.

8.7 Example: the senso_hedo_cocktail dataset
The senso_hedo_cocktail dataset contains the sensory evaluations of 16 cocktails described by 13 attributes, as well as individual liking scores from 100 consumers. It is used to illustrate the construction of a preference map: the sensory space is first constructed by PCA in MEDA, then the hedonic scores are projected into it through this function. The numerical values and graphics discussed below come directly from the analysis results. To load this dataset, open jamovi, click the icon in the top left corner, the three stacked lines, then Open → Data Library → SEDA.

The PCA produces a two-dimensional space: Dim. 1 explains 53.25% of the variance and Dim. 2 explains 24.13%, that is, 77.37% cumulative. The 1/2 plane therefore summarises the sensory profiles of the cocktails well.
The automatic description of the dimensions confirms the interpretation of the axes:

Dim. 1 opposes acidity (correlation 0.93), bitterness (0.88), odor.orange (0.75), and intensity (0.73) on one side, to odor.banana (-0.93), sweet (-0.93), thickness (-0.88), and pulp (-0.70) on the other. This is a clear opposition between acidic and intense cocktails vs sweet, thick, banana-like cocktails.
Dim. 2 is more strongly structured by odor.lemon (0.77), odor.mango (0.69), persistence (0.66), and color.intensity (0.58), with odor.orange (-0.61) on the negative side.

On the individual map, the cocktails are widely distributed across the plane. 386 is located in the upper right (high on Dim. 2), 131 at the bottom centre, 447 and 312 on the left (sweet, thick), and 194, 233, and 245 on the right (acidic, intense). Once the PCA has been run, the Dim. 1 and Dim. 2 columns automatically appear in the jamovi data sheet.


8.7.3 Step 2 — Construct the preference map in SEDA
Return to SEDA > Hedonic Data > Preference Mapping and use the saved coordinates as X-axis and Y-axis. Select the hedonic columns in Liking Variables, keep Regression model = Quadratic, and use Preference threshold (SD) = 0.
To reproduce the segment-based reading as well, enable Classification of consumers, leave Number of clusters = -1, and keep Cluster dendrogram and Preference maps by cluster checked. Enabling classification does not change the overall map; it adds complementary results about consumer heterogeneity.


8.7.4 Analysis of the Overall Preference Map graph
The resulting map superimposes the preference surface onto the position of the 16 cocktails in the sensory space. The dark red area — corresponding to more than 80–90% favourable consumers — is located on the left of the plane, in the region with negative coordinates on Dim. 1, where the cocktails 182, 444, 343, and 447 are located. These cocktails, characterised by sweeter, thicker, banana-like profiles, lie in a high-preference region.
Conversely, the blue area — corresponding to fewer than 20% favourable consumers — is located on the right of the plane, where the cocktails 194, 233, and 245 are located, characterised by acidic and intense profiles.
The cocktails 131 (bottom centre) and 386 (upper right) are located in intermediate to low-preference areas (light blue, 10–25%).


8.7.5 Reading the consumer classification
With Number of clusters = -1, the Ward classification applied to the centred liking profiles retains 2 consumer clusters in this example:

Cluster 1: 62 consumers (62.0%). The products with the highest relative liking in the centred cluster profile are 182, 447, 472.
Cluster 2: 38 consumers (38.0%). The products with the highest relative liking in the centred cluster profile are 343, 312, 182.

Product 182 appears among the highest relative liking values in both clusters, whereas 447/472 distinguish Cluster 1 and 343/312 distinguish Cluster 2 among the observed cocktails. This gives a concrete first indication of both shared and segment-specific preference patterns.
These short descriptions are based on the mean centred liking profile within each cluster. They identify which tested products most distinguish the relative preferences of a segment; they do not, by themselves, assign a sensory meaning to that segment.
Use Consumer Cluster Sizes to assess the weight of each segment and Consumer Cluster Membership to identify the consumers composing it. The Consumer Cluster Dendrogram shows the hierarchy underlying the partition.
The Preference Maps by Consumer Cluster should then be compared in the common sensory space. Because every cluster map uses exactly the same product coordinates, regression model, and preference threshold as the overall map, differences between maps reflect heterogeneity in predicted preference patterns rather than a change of reference space. Very small clusters should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously.


8.7.6 Synthetic interpretation
The sensory space structured by the PCA, based on the acidic-intense vs sweet-thick opposition, is directly readable on the preference map. The highest-preference region lies on the sweet-thick side, whereas acidic and intense profiles are less appreciated. No cocktail appears to occupy the centre of this highest-preference region, which suggests a direction for formulation improvement rather than an already optimal product.

What we take away from this example: preference mapping directly links the sensory space and hedonic preferences, making it possible to identify a favourable region of the product space even when no existing product occupies its centre.

8.9 Practical tips

Always check that X-axis and Y-axis come from the same representation space and refer to the same stimuli as the liking scores.
Use individual scores in Liking Variables, one column per consumer.
Start with Preference threshold (SD) = 0; then vary it to assess whether high-preference regions remain stable.

title: 8  Hedonic Data — Preference Mapping
text:
8.10 In summary
Preference mapping links a two-dimensional stimulus space to individual liking scores. SEDA fits a preference surface for each consumer, standardises the predictions, and represents the proportion of consumers exceeding Preference threshold (SD) in each region of the plane. The overall map can be complemented by Ward clustering of centred liking profiles and by cluster-specific preference maps. The analysis can therefore distinguish a broadly shared preference region from an overall pattern that hides several consumer segments, while keeping the same product space for all comparisons.
